answers.text: The changes stayed in flash memory, which failed and needs replacing before changes can be kept.
answers.rationale: Flash memory saves the Operating System (OS) loaded at boot; configuration changes are stored in the running-configuration in Random Access Memory (RAM).

answers.text: The changes stayed in Read Only Memory (ROM) and needed saving to its boot up routines.
answers.rationale: Read Only Memory (ROM) holds the diagnostic and boot up routines as burned-in memory that cannot be accessed or changed.

answers.text: The changes stayed in Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) and needed copying into Random Access Memory (RAM) before the reboot.
answers.rationale: Configuration changes go to the running-configuration in Random Access Memory (RAM); Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) saves the startup-configuration, which is loaded into RAM at boot.

questions.stem: A switch needs a newer Operating System (OS) version. An airman proposes writing the new version into Read Only Memory (ROM), since the switch runs its boot up routines from there at every start. MSgt Rush must decide where the new version belongs so the switch loads it at boot. Which decision is best supported?

keywords.text: so the switch loads it at boot

answers.text: Place it in Read Only Memory (ROM), since the switch runs its boot up routines from there.
answers.rationale: Read Only Memory (ROM) holds the boot up routines as burned-in memory that cannot be accessed or changed, so a new version cannot be written there.

answers.text: Place it in Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM), since it keeps data for long term storage.
answers.rationale: Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) saves the startup-configuration; the Operating System (OS) is saved in flash memory.

answers.text: Place it in Random Access Memory (RAM), since it is the running memory for operations.
answers.rationale: Random Access Memory (RAM) is the running memory that the Operating System (OS) is loaded into at boot, not where the OS is saved.

answers.text: Place it in flash memory, since the switch loads its saved Operating System (OS) from there at boot.
answers.rationale: Flash memory is where the Operating System (OS) is saved and is accessed at every boot, while Read Only Memory (ROM) cannot be changed.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush is documenting a network that mixes Cisco and non-Cisco switches, and each switch must learn its neighbors' system names and management addresses. An airman proposes Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP), since the core switches are Cisco devices. MSgt Rush must choose the protocol. Which choice is best supported?

answers.text: Use Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP), since it shares information between directly connected devices.
answers.rationale: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) is Cisco proprietary and shares information between directly connected Cisco devices, so the non-Cisco switches are left out.

answers.text: Use Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP), since it is vendor neutral and advertises system names.
answers.rationale: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) is vendor neutral and stores and advertises details such as system names and the management Internet Protocol (IP) address.

answers.text: Use Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), since switches use it to communicate with each other.
answers.rationale: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) lets switches communicate to discover physical loops; it does not share system names or management addresses with neighbors.

answers.text: Use 802.1Q, since it is the non-proprietary method for tagging trunk frames.
answers.rationale: 802.1Q tags frames with a Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) header on trunks; it does not share system names with neighbors.

questions.stem: After a broadcast storm took down a building network, an airman proposes removing every redundant link between its switches so that no loop can form. MSgt Rush wants to keep the backup paths that protect against a single point of failure. Which course of action is best supported?

answers.text: Keep the redundant links and run Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) to build a loop-free logical topology.
answers.rationale: Redundant links are necessary in a network, and Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) specifies an algorithm that switches use to create a loop-free logical topology.

answers.text: Remove the redundant links, since a loop is a second path to a destination device.
answers.rationale: Redundant links overcome a single point of failure and are necessary in a network, so removing them brings that single point of failure back.

answers.text: Keep the redundant links and run Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD) to shut down looping ports.
answers.rationale: Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD) shuts down the port of a switch having trouble hearing on a one-way link; it does not build a loop-free topology.

answers.text: Keep the redundant links and run Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) to advertise each path.
answers.rationale: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) advertises data and Layer 2 configurations to adjacent nodes; it does not prevent loops.

questions.stem: A bad transmitter on a link between two switches means only one of them still receives the other's traffic, so the backup switch stops hearing its partner and may start forwarding. An airman proposes relying on Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) alone. MSgt Rush wants the affected port shut down to prevent errors. Which feature meets that requirement?

keywords.text: only one of them still receives the other's traffic

answers.text: Loopguard, since it acts on links where traffic fails one way.
answers.rationale: Loopguard also addresses one-way links, but it places the port in a loop inconsistent state instead of shutting it down.

answers.text: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), since it discovers physical loops between switches.
answers.rationale: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) discovers physical loops and builds a loop-free topology; it does not shut down the port of a switch that cannot hear.

answers.text: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP), since it advertises Layer 2 configurations to neighbors.
answers.rationale: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) advertises data and Layer 2 configurations to adjacent nodes; it does not act on a one-way link.

answers.text: Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD), since it acts on links where traffic fails one way.
answers.rationale: This is a unidirectional link, and Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD) causes the switch that is having trouble hearing to shut down the port.

questions.stem: A switch at a busy point in the network must start forwarding each frame without first storing the entire frame, and MSgt Rush wants one fixed switching method that still keeps frames damaged by fragmentation from being passed along. An airman proposes Store-and-Forward so that every frame is checked in full. Which switching method is best supported?

keywords.text: without first storing the entire frame

answers.rationale: Store-and-Forward stores the entire frame in internal memory before forwarding, which this switch must not do.

answers.text: Cut-Through, since it copies the destination Media Access Control (MAC) address alone and reduces latency.
answers.rationale: Cut-Through reduces latency, but bad frames are forwarded, so damaged frames would be passed along.

answers.text: Fragment-Free, since it stores the leading 64 bytes of each frame before forwarding.
answers.rationale: Fragment-Free is a hybrid that stores the first 64 bytes before forwarding, and that is where frame fragmentation is most likely to happen.
Adaptive switching changes the method with traffic conditions, so it is not the one fixed method MSgt Rush wants.

questions.stem: A switch feeds a segment where frames corrupted anywhere in the frame keep forcing destinations to request resends. MSgt Rush wants every bad frame discarded at the switch, not only those damaged by fragmentation. An airman proposes Cut-Through because it reduces latency. Which switching method is best supported?

keywords.text: frames corrupted anywhere in the frame

answers.text: Cut-Through, since it reduces latency by copying just the destination address.
answers.rationale: Cut-Through forwards bad frames, and the destination then has to request that the source send the frame again.
Store-and-Forward stores the entire frame and checks it with a Cyclical Redundancy Check (CRC), and a frame with an error is discarded.

answers.text: Fragment-Free, since it discards a frame when fragmentation is found.
answers.rationale: Fragment-Free only checks the first 64 bytes, where fragmentation is most likely, so it does not check each whole frame.
Adaptive switching selects a method with traffic conditions, so it may pick Cut-Through, which forwards bad frames.

questions.stem: A printer was just cabled to a switch and has sent no frames since. An airman watching the switch sees a computer's frame to the printer go out every active port except the one it came in on, and the airman proposes replacing the switch as faulty. MSgt Rush must explain the behavior. Which explanation is best supported?

answers.text: The switch floods it, since it records a device's address when that device transmits a frame.
answers.rationale: The switch learns a device's address from the source of a frame it transmits, and a frame whose destination is not in the table is flooded.

answers.text: The switch is faulty, since a working switch forwards frames out the host's interface alone.
answers.rationale: A switch forwards a frame out the host's interface once that destination is listed in its Media Access Control (MAC) address table, and the silent printer is not listed.

answers.text: The switch is in a broadcast storm, since its frames are rebroadcast back onto the network.
answers.rationale: A broadcast storm builds as other devices rebroadcast data until the whole network is overwhelmed; one flooded frame is not that.

answers.text: The switch floods it, since it repeats each frame out the other interfaces.
answers.rationale: Repeating each frame out all other interfaces is how a hub works; a switch floods a frame whose destination is not in its table.

questions.stem: After an airman added a second cable between two switches as a backup, the Media Access Control (MAC) address table on one switch keeps changing the interface listed for a file server, and the network slows, though communication has not failed. The airman suspects a cabling fault on the server and plans to replace its cable. MSgt Rush must name the more likely cause. Which diagnosis is best supported?

keywords.text: keeps changing the interface listed for a file server

answers.text: Diagnose a broadcast storm, since devices rebroadcast data until the network is overwhelmed.
answers.rationale: A broadcast storm overwhelms the whole network and leads to the failure of network communication, which has not happened here.

answers.text: Diagnose a late collision, since another system transmits after the first 64 bytes.
answers.rationale: A late collision means another system transmitted after a host sent its first 64 bytes; it does not move a device's location in the table.

answers.text: Diagnose a unidirectional link, since traffic in one of the two directions has failed.
answers.rationale: A unidirectional link occurs when traffic in one direction fails; the server's frames are arriving, over two paths.

answers.text: Diagnose multiple frame copies, since the server's frames now arrive over two paths.
answers.rationale: The second cable gives more than one path, so copies of a frame arrive from different segments and the Media Access Control (MAC) address table is confused and constantly updated.

questions.stem: A switch port's counters show both ordinary collisions and late collisions. An airman proposes opening a trouble ticket for each collision on the port. MSgt Rush must decide which counter points to a problem worth troubleshooting. Which decision is best supported?

answers.text: Troubleshoot the ordinary collisions, since each one signals an error condition.
answers.rationale: Collisions are a part of Ethernet communications and do not imply any error condition, so ordinary collisions need no ticket.

answers.text: Troubleshoot neither counter, since collisions are a normal part of Ethernet.
answers.rationale: Ordinary collisions are normal, but late collisions can be caused by faulty network devices on the segment and duplex mismatches.

answers.text: Troubleshoot the late collisions, since ordinary collisions imply no error condition.
answers.rationale: Collisions are a part of Ethernet and imply no error, while late collisions can be caused by faulty network devices and duplex mismatches.

answers.text: Troubleshoot neither counter, since a switch port is its own collision domain.
answers.rationale: A switch port being its own collision domain does not make late collisions normal; they can come from faulty devices or duplex mismatches.

questions.stem: A flat switched network serves two workgroups, and broadcasts from one workgroup reach every computer in both. An airman proposes adding more switches, since each switch port is already its own collision domain. MSgt Rush wants each workgroup's broadcasts kept within that workgroup without adding a Layer 3 device. Which plan is best supported?

answers.text: Add more switches, since each switch port is its own collision domain.
answers.rationale: A port's own collision domain does not filter broadcasts, which pass through the switches until they reach a Layer 3 device.

answers.text: Place each workgroup in a Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since switches segment those broadcasts.
answers.rationale: Switches used with Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) segment a network into smaller broadcast domains; without VLANs, broadcasts pass until a Layer 3 device.

answers.text: Set each port to wire speed, since that matches the media (cable) speed.
answers.rationale: Wire speed adjusts a port's bandwidth to the cable speed; it does not keep a workgroup's broadcasts within that workgroup.

answers.text: Place a router between the workgroups, since it forwards Internet Protocol (IP) packets between networks.
answers.rationale: A router is a Layer 3 device, and MSgt Rush ruled out adding a Layer 3 device.

questions.stem: An airman is setting up a switch that will connect a workgroup's computers, and nobody will manage it remotely. He insists the switch needs an Internet Protocol (IP) address before it can forward frames between the computers. MSgt Rush must answer before the switch goes into service. Which response is best supported?

answers.text: Forwarding needs each device's Media Access Control (MAC) address, since it identifies the device.
answers.rationale: A switch identifies each connected device by its 48-bit Media Access Control (MAC) address, and its Internet Protocol (IP) address is needed for logging in to make configuration changes.

answers.text: Forwarding needs an Internet Protocol (IP) address, since the switch makes Layer 3 decisions.
answers.rationale: Switches move frames at Layer 2 (Data Link Layer), and the Internet Protocol (IP) address is needed only to log in for configuration changes.

answers.text: Forwarding needs a subnet mask, since it splits each address into network and host parts.
answers.rationale: A subnet mask divides an Internet Protocol (IP) address into network and host addresses; a switch forwards frames at Layer 2.

answers.text: Forwarding needs a console password, since Department of Defense (DoD) policy requires one.
answers.rationale: Department of Defense (DoD) policy calls for console port password protection to prevent unauthorized changes; it does not affect forwarding frames.

questions.stem: One switch holds the Sales Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 10 and the Marketing VLAN 20. An airman finds that a Sales host cannot reach a Marketing host and argues that hosts on one switch should talk directly, so the switch must be faulty. MSgt Rush must explain the result. Which explanation is best supported?

keywords.text: argues that hosts on one switch should talk directly

answers.text: The switch is faulty, since all hosts on one switch share a single broadcast domain whatever their Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN).
answers.rationale: Each Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) is its own single broadcast domain, and VLANs can exist on a single switch, so one switch can hold two separate domains.

answers.text: The switch is working, since traffic between Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) must pass through a Layer 3 routing process.
answers.rationale: Each Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) is a single broadcast domain, even when they share one switch, and communication between VLANs must go through a Layer 3 routing process.

answers.text: The switch needs a trunk between the host ports, since a trunk merges Sales and Marketing into one Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN).
answers.rationale: A trunk is a connection that can carry more than one Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN); it carries the VLANs side by side and does not merge them into one.

answers.text: The switch needs an Internet Protocol (IP) address on each host port, since that address lets ports reach another Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN).
answers.rationale: An Internet Protocol (IP) address on a switch is solely for remote access and is not for a particular port, so it cannot join two Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs).

questions.stem: Research and Sales hosts share one switch, and every port is still in default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1. An airman notes that Sales hosts see every broadcast the Research hosts send and proposes moving Research to a second switch cabled to the first, still in VLAN 1. MSgt Rush must keep Research frames away from Sales hosts. Which plan is best supported?

keywords.text: Sales hosts see every broadcast the Research hosts send

answers.text: Move Research to a second switch in Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1, since separate hardware splits the broadcast domain.
answers.rationale: Every broadcast frame on a segment is seen by all its devices, and Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1 on both connected switches still forms one local network.

answers.text: Rename Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1 to Research, since a descriptive name limits which hosts receive its frames.
answers.rationale: A descriptive name such as "Sales" is only a better name than the default; every host stays in the same Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1 broadcast domain, so Sales hosts still see Research broadcasts.

answers.text: Give the switch an Internet Protocol (IP) address in Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1, since that address filters frames by port.
answers.rationale: An Internet Protocol (IP) address on a switch is solely for remote access and is not for a particular port, so it filters no frames.

answers.text: Place Research in its own Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since only devices in the same VLAN receive its frames.
answers.rationale: Every broadcast frame on a segment is seen by all devices on it, while security increases because only devices in the same Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) receive the frame.

questions.stem: An airman creates a Research Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) numbered 30 on an access switch and a Research VLAN numbered 31 on the connected distribution switch, then claims the matching names make them one local network. MSgt Rush needs the Research hosts on both switches in one broadcast domain. Which action is best supported?

keywords.text: claims the matching names make them one local network

answers.text: Use Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 30 on both switches, since the number identifies the VLAN in all systems.
answers.rationale: Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) are identified by number in all systems, and VLAN 30 created on connected switches is treated as a single local network.

answers.text: Keep Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) 30 and 31, since matching descriptive names join them into one local network.
answers.rationale: Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) are identified by number, which is referenced in all systems; a descriptive name is only a better name than the default and does not join VLANs 30 and 31.

answers.text: Route between Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) 30 and 31, since a Layer 3 routing process merges them into one domain.
answers.rationale: Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) keep one VLAN's broadcasts from another, so routing between VLANs 30 and 31 connects two broadcast domains without merging them.

answers.text: Assign both groups to the default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since each switch already has that VLAN created.
answers.rationale: Ports should never be assigned to the default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) on any network for security, so VLAN 1 is the wrong place for the Research hosts.

questions.stem: A new trunk must link a Cisco access switch to a distribution switch from another manufacturer. An airman plans to use Inter-Switch Link (ISL) because it tags every frame that crosses the trunk. MSgt Rush must pick the trunking method and state how it tags frames. Which choice is best supported?

answers.text: Use Inter-Switch Link (ISL), since it adds a new header and trailer to each frame.
answers.rationale: Inter-Switch Link (ISL) does add a new header and trailer, but it is a deprecated Cisco proprietary method, so it does not suit a trunk to another manufacturer's switch.

answers.text: Use Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.1q, since it adds a new header and trailer to each frame.
answers.rationale: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.1q is the open standard, but it uses space in the standard frame header; Inter-Switch Link (ISL) adds the header and trailer.

answers.text: Use Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.1q, since it tags each frame in existing header space.
answers.rationale: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.1q is the open standard for trunks, and it tags a frame by using existing space in the standard frame header.

answers.text: Use Inter-Switch Link (ISL), since it tags each frame in existing header space.
answers.rationale: Inter-Switch Link (ISL) is a deprecated Cisco proprietary method, and it adds a new header and trailer instead of using the existing frame header.

questions.stem: After installing a switch, an airman shuts down its unused ports but leaves them in Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1, noting that nobody ever changed their membership and that a shut-down port carries nothing. MSgt Rush must finish securing those ports to reduce vulnerabilities. Which action is best supported?

keywords.text: leaves them in Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1

answers.text: Leave the ports in default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1, since a shut-down port carries no traffic.
answers.rationale: Ports stay in default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1 until changed, and ports should never be assigned to the default VLAN on any network, even when shut down.

answers.text: Assign the ports to an inactive Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since unused ports never belong in default VLAN 1.
answers.rationale: Unused ports should be shut down and assigned to an inactive Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), and ports should never be assigned to the default VLAN on any network for security.

answers.text: Assign the ports to the management Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since that VLAN never carries user traffic.
answers.rationale: The management Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) serves telnet, Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and syslog, and best practice prunes unnecessary ports from it; unused ports go to an inactive VLAN.

answers.text: Assign the ports to the Sales Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since only Sales devices then receive their frames.
answers.rationale: Limiting frames to Sales devices does not remove the vulnerability; unused ports should be shut down and assigned to an inactive Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), not an active user VLAN.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush wants to manage a switch remotely with telnet and send its syslog messages to a logging server. An airman proposes assigning an Internet Protocol (IP) address to the access port of MSgt Rush's workstation in the Sales Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN). Which plan for the address is best supported?

keywords.text: assigning an Internet Protocol (IP) address to the access port

answers.text: Assign the address to the workstation's access port, since remote access runs through that one port.
answers.rationale: An Internet Protocol (IP) address on a switch is solely for remote access to the switch and is not for a particular port.

answers.text: Assign the address to the switch on the Sales Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since management and user data belong together.
answers.rationale: Best practice separates in-band management, device protocol and data traffic, so the address belongs on the management Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), not the Sales VLAN.

answers.text: Assign the address to the switch on the management Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since telnet and syslog use that VLAN.
answers.rationale: A switch's Internet Protocol (IP) address is for remote access, not a particular port, and the management Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) is used for telnet and syslog.

answers.text: Assign the address to the trunk port, since a trunk carries more than one Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) to the switch.
answers.rationale: A trunk does carry more than one Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), but a switch's Internet Protocol (IP) address is not for a particular port.

questions.stem: Sales Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) frames cross a trunk between two switches and then reach a Sales workstation on an access port. An airman sees no VLAN tag in the frames the workstation receives, argues that the trunk is not tagging, and wants the trunk rebuilt. Which response from MSgt Rush is best supported?

keywords.text: sees no VLAN tag in the frames the workstation receives

answers.text: Rebuild the trunk, since a tagged frame keeps its tag until it reaches the workstation.
answers.rationale: A Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) tag is removed when the frame is placed on an access port, so an untagged frame at the workstation is expected.

answers.text: Rebuild the trunk, since the switch copies each tag into its Media Access Control (MAC) address table for the workstation.
answers.rationale: The switch places a frame's source address and interface ID in its Media Access Control (MAC) address table; the Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) tag itself is removed at the access port.

answers.text: Keep the trunk, since a trunk passes Sales frames along without applying a tag.
answers.rationale: A Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) tag is applied when an Ethernet frame crosses a trunk; the frame loses that tag only when it is placed on the access port.

answers.text: Keep the trunk, since the tag applied on the trunk is removed at the access port.
answers.rationale: A Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) tag is applied when an Ethernet frame crosses a trunk and removed when the frame is placed on an access port, so the workstation sees no tag.

questions.stem: A new Sales host must stay at its desk on another floor, where its port connects to a different access switch than the other Sales hosts. An airman proposes moving the host to the Sales hosts' switch so it can join their broadcast domain. MSgt Rush must decide. Which action is best supported?

keywords.text: proposes moving the host to the Sales hosts' switch

answers.text: Assign its port to the Sales Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since a VLAN spans switches regardless of physical location.
answers.rationale: Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) add only the devices wanted to a broadcast domain regardless of physical location, and a VLAN can span multiple switches.

answers.text: Move the host to the Sales switch, since Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) membership follows the switch where hosts sit.
answers.rationale: A Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) can span multiple switches, and devices join it wherever they sit, so the host need not move.

answers.text: Assign its port to a new Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) routed to Sales, since routing places both in one broadcast domain.
answers.rationale: Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) keep one VLAN's broadcasts from another; routing connects two VLANs but leaves them separate broadcast domains.

answers.text: Leave its port in default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 1, since VLAN 1 already exists on both switches.
answers.rationale: Ports should never be assigned to the default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) on any network for security, and VLAN 1 is not the Sales broadcast domain.

questions.stem: The link between an access switch and a distribution switch must carry the Sales Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 10 and the Marketing VLAN 20. An airman configures both link ports as access ports in VLAN 10, arguing that VLAN tags will keep the Marketing frames separate. Which change should MSgt Rush make?

keywords.text: configures both link ports as access ports in VLAN 10

answers.text: Keep both access ports, since tags keep Marketing frames separate on the link.
answers.rationale: An access port is a member of only one Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), and the tag is removed when a frame is placed on it, so it cannot carry VLAN 20.

answers.text: Give the switch an Internet Protocol (IP) address on Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 20, since it lets Marketing use the link.
answers.rationale: An Internet Protocol (IP) address on a switch is solely for remote access, so it does not let Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) 20 cross an access link.

answers.text: Make the link a trunk, since an access port holds one Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) and a trunk carries several.
answers.rationale: An access port is a member of only one Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), while a trunk is a connection between network devices that can carry more than one VLAN.

answers.text: Make both link ports members of the default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN), since that VLAN carries both groups.
answers.rationale: Ports should never be assigned to the default Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) on any network for security, and VLAN 1 is a separate VLAN that carries neither group.

questions.stem: At power-up, a router runs its bootstrap program, its hardware interfaces pass their tests, and then it halts with a message that no Internetwork Operating System (IOS) image was found. An airman proposes replacing the Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM), since it holds the startup-configuration file. MSgt Rush must name the component to examine. Which choice is best supported?

keywords.text: no Internetwork Operating System (IOS) image was found

answers.text: Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM), since the startup-configuration is read before the Operating System (OS) loads.
answers.rationale: The startup-configuration is copied from Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) after the Operating System (OS) is loaded, so it does not explain a missing OS image.

answers.text: Read Only Memory (ROM), since it holds the Operating System (OS) image that the router runs.
answers.rationale: Read Only Memory (ROM) holds the diagnostic and boot up routines, and the bootstrap from it already ran and tested the hardware.

answers.text: Random Access Memory (RAM), since it holds the copy of the Operating System (OS) that the router runs.
answers.rationale: Random Access Memory (RAM) is the working memory that receives a copy of the Operating System (OS) after loading, so an image that was never found points to where it is stored.

answers.text: Flash memory, since the Internetwork Operating System (IOS) is loaded from it into Random Access Memory (RAM).
answers.rationale: After the bootstrap from Read Only Memory (ROM) tests the hardware, the Internetwork Operating System (IOS) is loaded from flash memory, which holds it, into Random Access Memory (RAM).

questions.stem: Two Air Force Bases each run their network as a separate Autonomous System (AS) with its own routing policy, and MSgt Rush must link them so they exchange routes. An airman suggests extending Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) across both bases, since its backbone already carries routing information between areas. Which protocol is best supported for the link?

keywords.text: separate Autonomous System (AS) with its own routing policy

answers.text: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), since its backbone distributes routing information between areas.
answers.rationale: Areas are divisions inside one Autonomous System (AS), so a backbone that distributes routing information between areas does not join two separate autonomous systems.

answers.text: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), since it exchanges routing information between Autonomous Systems (ASs).
answers.rationale: The primary function of Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is exchanging routing information between Autonomous Systems (ASs), and routers moving information between autonomous systems use exterior gateway protocols such as BGP.

answers.text: Routing Information Protocol (RIP), since its updates travel to directly connected neighbor routers.
answers.rationale: Routing Information Protocol (RIP) updates stop at directly connected neighbors; nothing in that behavior exchanges routes between Autonomous Systems (ASs), which calls for an exterior gateway protocol.
Scaling to large networks does not make a protocol exterior; routers that move information between Autonomous Systems (ASs) use exterior gateway protocols.

questions.stem: A new workstation reaches hosts on its own subnet but nothing on other networks. An airman finds its default gateway set to a router interface on a different subnet, two routers away, and proposes keeping it because that router leads toward the Internet. MSgt Rush must decide the setting. Which choice is best supported?

keywords.text: its default gateway set to a router interface on a different subnet

answers.text: Keep the remote router interface, since that router leads toward the Internet that the new workstation needs.
answers.rationale: A router interface on a different subnet, two routers away, is not on the workstation's subnet, so the workstation has no local router to hand traffic for other networks to.

answers.text: Use the switch on the workstation's subnet, since the switch connects the hosts there.
answers.rationale: Switching is a Layer 2 function, while the default gateway is an address on a Layer 3 network device.

answers.text: Use the nearest router interface on the workstation's subnet, since it is the access point to the network.
answers.rationale: A default gateway is the address on a Layer 3 device that serves as the access point to or from a network, and that address is the nearest router interface on the subnet.

answers.text: Use the border router on the Wide Area Network (WAN) side, since it connects the base to the WAN.
answers.rationale: A border router connects a Local Area Network (LAN) with the Wide Area Network (WAN), but its far-side address is not on the workstation's subnet, so the workstation cannot hand traffic to it directly.

questions.stem: One flat Local Area Network (LAN) segment holds two squadrons, and broadcasts from each squadron reach every host on it. MSgt Rush wants each squadron's broadcasts kept to its own hosts. An airman proposes connecting both squadrons to a single router interface, since routers break up broadcast domains. Which design is best supported?

keywords.text: each squadron's broadcasts kept to its own hosts

answers.text: Connect both squadrons to one router interface, since the router breaks up broadcast domains.
answers.rationale: Each router interface is one broadcast domain, so two squadrons behind one interface still share their broadcasts.

answers.text: Join the squadrons through a hub, since the hub separates the traffic on its ports.
answers.rationale: A hub transmits each message out of every port, so it spreads the broadcasts to both squadrons.

answers.text: Keep one segment and rely on Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), since the destination host alone replies.
answers.rationale: An Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) broadcast is still received and processed by all devices on the segment, even though one host replies.

answers.text: Put each squadron on its own router interface, since each interface is a separate broadcast domain.
answers.rationale: Each interface on a router is a separate broadcast domain, and broadcasts stop at the router, so each squadron's broadcasts stay with its own hosts.

questions.stem: An airman captures the same packet on the first and last links of a path that crosses three routers. The source and destination Media Access Control (MAC) addresses differ between the two captures, while the Internet Protocol (IP) addresses match. The airman claims a device tampered with the packet. MSgt Rush must judge the claim. Which conclusion is best supported?

keywords.text: Media Access Control (MAC) addresses differ between the two captures

answers.text: Tampering, since a packet keeps its Media Access Control (MAC) addresses from source to destination.
answers.rationale: Media Access Control (MAC) addresses carry information from one Layer 2 interface to the next, so they change at each hop and do not stay fixed end to end.

answers.text: Normal forwarding, since each hop changes the Layer 2 addresses while the Layer 3 addresses stay constant.
answers.rationale: As a packet crosses an internetwork its Layer 2 addresses change while its Network Layer addresses stay constant, because physical addresses serve one link and logical addresses serve network to network.

answers.text: Normal forwarding, since each hop changes the Layer 3 addresses while the Layer 2 addresses stay the same.
answers.rationale: This reverses the behavior, and the captures show the Internet Protocol (IP) addresses matching while the hardware addresses differ.

answers.text: Tampering, since the Internet Protocol (IP) addresses should have changed at each router.
answers.rationale: Logical addresses such as Internet Protocol (IP) addresses carry information from one network to another and stay constant across the path.

questions.stem: Small packets from a squadron reach a remote server, but each large packet is discarded at the router where the path enters a data link with a smaller Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU). An airman suggests the packets' Time to Live (TTL) is expiring at that router. MSgt Rush must name the cause. Which cause is best supported?

keywords.text: each large packet is discarded at the router

answers.text: The packets' Time to Live (TTL) counter expires there, and the router discards them.
answers.rationale: A Time to Live (TTL) counter does not depend on packet size, yet the small packets cross the same router and arrive.

answers.text: The packets carry a wrong header version number, and the router discards them.
answers.rationale: A wrong version number gets a packet discarded whatever its size, but the small packets from the same squadron arrive.

answers.text: The packets must be fragmented there, and their allow fragmentation flag is not set.
answers.rationale: Fragmentation lets packets cross data links with smaller Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) sizes, and a packet that must be fragmented without the allow fragmentation flag set is discarded.

answers.text: The packets have Department of Defense (DoD) security bits set, and the server is not authorized.
answers.rationale: Department of Defense (DoD) security bits are not tied to packet size or to one data link, so they do not explain why only large packets fail at that router.

questions.stem: An airman's network inventory lists Internet Protocol (IP) and Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) together as routing protocols that carry user data between networks. MSgt Rush must correct the entry before it goes into the squadron's documentation. Which correction is best supported?

answers.text: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is routed, carrying the messages; Internet Protocol (IP) is routing, delivering them.
answers.rationale: This reverses the roles: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is a link state routing protocol, and Internet Protocol (IP) is a routed protocol.

answers.text: Both are routing protocols as listed; each builds and maintains routing tables.
answers.rationale: Internet Protocol (IP) does not build routing tables; it is a routed protocol that provides connectionless delivery of packets.

answers.text: Internet Protocol (IP) is routed, carrying the messages; Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is routing, delivering them.
answers.rationale: Internet Protocol (IP) is a routed protocol, Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is a link state routing protocol, and routed protocols are messages that routing protocols deliver.

answers.text: Both are routed protocols; each supplies the logical addressing that routers use.
answers.rationale: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) does not supply logical addressing to packets; it is a routing protocol that sends the state of its links to the routers in its area.

questions.stem: Users report that a remote server is unreachable, and the source host receives Destination Unreachable messages about its packets. An airman says the Internet Protocol (IP) itself generated those messages, since IP delivered the packets. MSgt Rush must identify what produced the reports before troubleshooting further. Which choice is best supported?

answers.text: Internet Protocol (IP), since it delivers each packet and reports the failures to the source.
answers.rationale: Internet Protocol (IP) gives connectionless, best-effort delivery and does not report routing anomalies back to the source.

answers.text: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), since Internet Protocol (IP) leaves error reporting to it.
answers.rationale: Internet Protocol (IP) does not report errors back to the source; Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) does, and Destination Unreachable is one of the messages it generates.

answers.text: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), since it resolves the server's network address to a hardware address.
answers.rationale: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps network addresses to hardware addresses; it does not send error messages about packet processing to the source.

answers.text: The Hello protocol, since its keep-alives report that a connected router has stopped working.
answers.rationale: Hello messages act as keep-alives between connected routers; they do not send error reports about a host's packets back to that host.

questions.stem: After the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routers on a base have acquired their neighbors, an airman proposes filtering further Hello packets on a busy link, since neighbor discovery is complete. MSgt Rush must decide whether the Hello traffic can be removed. Which decision is best supported?

keywords.text: filtering further Hello packets on a busy link

answers.text: Filter the Hello packets, since their job is acquiring neighbors at power-up, and that job is now done.
answers.rationale: Acquiring neighbors is one role of Hello packets; they also tell routers that the neighbor and the link between them remain functional, so filtering them removes that check.

answers.text: Keep the Hello packets, since they also act as keep-alives showing the neighbor and link still work.
answers.rationale: Hello packets acquire neighbors and also act as a keep-alive that lets routers know the neighbor router and the link between them are still functional.

answers.text: Filter the Hello packets, since the topology table already records each neighbor.
answers.rationale: The topology table holds the Link State Advertisements (LSAs) from routers in the area, and listing a neighbor does not show that the link is functional.

answers.text: Keep the Hello packets, since they carry each router's routing table to its neighbors.
answers.rationale: Sending the entire routing table to neighbors describes distance vector updates, not Hello packets.

questions.stem: A router learns two paths to the same remote network: one from a static route and one from Routing Information Protocol (RIP). The static source has the lower administrative distance, while the RIP path has the lower hop count. An airman predicts the router will use the RIP path. MSgt Rush must predict which path is used. Which prediction is best supported?

keywords.text: The static source has the lower administrative distance

answers.text: The Routing Information Protocol (RIP) path, since hop count decides between paths from different sources.
answers.rationale: Hop count is a metric for rating paths, but between routing sources the router chooses by administrative distance, where the static source is lower.

answers.text: The Routing Information Protocol (RIP) path, since its periodic updates make it the newer information.
answers.rationale: The router's choice among sources is not set by which update arrived last; it rests on which source is more trustworthy.

answers.text: The static route, since the lower administrative distance marks the more trustworthy source.
answers.rationale: With paths to the same destination from more than one routing source, routers choose the lowest administrative distance, and the lower it is, the more trustworthy the route.

answers.text: Neither path, since conflicting sources leave the router without a usable route.
answers.rationale: A router discards a packet when it has no listing to forward it, but here it holds two listings and picks one.

questions.stem: A detachment network has a few subnets whose layout and traffic pattern rarely change, and MSgt Rush wants no routing update traffic on its slow links. An airman recommends Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) so that routes adjust automatically. MSgt Rush must choose how the routers learn their paths. Which choice is best supported?

keywords.text: wants no routing update traffic on its slow links

answers.text: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), since its smaller updates are sent when the network topology changes.
answers.rationale: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) still exchanges routing updates between routers, which puts the traffic MSgt Rush wants to avoid on the slow links.

answers.text: Routing Information Protocol (RIP), since it is simple to understand and configure.
answers.rationale: Routing Information Protocol (RIP) sends broadcast routing updates every 30 seconds and on topology changes, which is update traffic on the slow links.
Scaling to large networks is not this network's need, and Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) still sends routing updates between routers.

answers.text: Static routes set by an administrator, since they suit a simple design with predictable traffic.
answers.rationale: Static routes are configured by hand, need no exchange of routing updates between routers, and work well where traffic is predictable and the design is simple.

questions.stem: A detachment router has routes for its two local subnets and one link to the base network, which connects onward to the other destinations users need. Packets for destinations the router has no listing for are being discarded. An airman proposes adding a separate static route for each remote network users visit. MSgt Rush wants one change that covers them all. Which change is best supported?

keywords.text: Packets for destinations the router has no listing for are being discarded

answers.text: Add a static route for each remote network, since each one sets the path to one more destination.
answers.rationale: Each static route covers one listed destination, so any network users visit later still has no listing and its packets are still discarded.

answers.text: Add a default route toward the base link, since packets with no known route are then sent there.
answers.rationale: A router discards a packet that has no usable listing, while a default route, the gateway of last resort, receives the packets that would otherwise be non-routable.

answers.text: Set a default gateway on each user host, since hosts then reach the detachment router.
answers.rationale: The packets already reach the detachment router; they are discarded there because the router itself has no listing for them.

answers.text: Set the allow fragmentation flag on the packets, since packets without it are discarded.
answers.rationale: That flag matters when a packet must be fragmented; the discards here follow from the missing routing-table listings.

questions.stem: On a base network with several redundant links, the routers use static routes. When one link fails, traffic keeps heading toward the failed link until an airman edits the routes, although a working alternate path exists. MSgt Rush wants the routers to shift to the alternate path on their own. Which change is best supported?

keywords.text: traffic keeps heading toward the failed link until an airman edits the routes

answers.text: Add more static routes, since each one gives the router another fixed path.
answers.rationale: Static routes do not change until the network administrator changes them, so more of them still need a manual edit after each failure.

answers.text: Add a default route, since it sends packets with no known route to one path.
answers.rationale: A default route serves only when no route to the destination is known, and the static route to the failed link is still listed.

answers.text: Lower the Time to Live (TTL) on the packets, since those headed to the failed link then expire sooner.
answers.rationale: An expired Time to Live (TTL) counter gets a packet discarded; it does not move traffic onto the alternate path.

answers.text: Move to dynamic routing, since routers recalculate from incoming routing status messages.
answers.rationale: Static routes do not change until the administrator changes them, while dynamic routing algorithms adjust to network changes by analyzing incoming routing status messages and recalculating routes.

questions.stem: Two paths connect a squadron to a data center. The first uses a high-bandwidth link that is busy for most of the day; the second uses a slower link that is lightly used. An airman wants the routers to prefer the first path at all times because its link has more bandwidth. MSgt Rush must judge the plan. Which judgment is best supported?

keywords.text: busy for most of the day

answers.text: Accept it, since bandwidth rates the maximum throughput that a link can attain, and the first link has more.
answers.rationale: Bandwidth rates a link's maximum throughput, but a faster link that is busier can be slower to deliver a packet, and the first link is the busy one.

answers.text: Reject it, since a busier faster link can take longer to deliver a packet than a slower link.
answers.rationale: Routes through links with greater bandwidth are not necessarily better, since a busier faster link can take longer, and load measures how busy a resource is.

answers.text: Accept it, since load measures the capacity of a link and not how busy it is.
answers.rationale: Load refers to how busy a network resource is, not to capacity, so the heavy use of the first link weighs against the plan.

answers.text: Reject it, since hop count is the metric that decides between the two paths.
answers.rationale: Hop count is one metric, but the stated difference between these paths is how busy each link is, not the number of hops.

questions.stem: A wing can send traffic between two sites over its own lines or over public lines billed for usage time. The public route has less delay, but the wing cares more about operating expenses than about speed. An airman proposes making delay the deciding routing metric. MSgt Rush must choose the metric. Which choice is best supported?

keywords.text: cares more about operating expenses than about speed

answers.text: Delay, since it measures the time needed to move a packet from source to destination through the internetwork.
answers.rationale: Delay measures transit time, which would favor the public lines that charge for usage, against the expense goal.

answers.text: Bandwidth, since it rates the available traffic capacity of each line.
answers.rationale: Bandwidth rates capacity, and capacity says nothing about the usage charges that the wing wants to avoid.

answers.text: Reliability, since it rates the dependability of each line by its bit-error rate.
answers.rationale: Reliability rates dependability by bit-error rate; the stated priority is operating expenses, not dependability.

answers.text: Communication cost, since it favors the wing's own lines even when their delay is longer.
answers.rationale: Communication cost serves organizations that care more about operating expenses than performance, sending packets over their own lines rather than public lines that cost money for usage time.

questions.stem: A base network running Routing Information Protocol (RIP) is growing, and some new destinations will sit more than 15 routers away from headquarters. An airman proposes moving to RIPv2, since it is the newer version. MSgt Rush must pick a protocol that can reach the whole network. Which choice is best supported?

answers.text: RIPv2, since it improves on the original by adding subnet masks to its updates.
answers.rationale: Adding subnet mask data allows variable length subnet masking, but the version still rates routes by hop count, so the distant destinations stay out of reach.

answers.text: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), since its hierarchical routing supports very large networks.
answers.rationale: Routing Information Protocol (RIP) is limited to 15 hops, which makes distance vector routing unsuitable for large networks, while Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) hierarchical routing supports very large networks.

answers.text: Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGRP), since it is built for interior gateway routing.
answers.rationale: Cisco developed Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) because Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGRP) had hop count limitations, so IGRP does not solve the distance problem.

answers.text: Routing Information Protocol (RIP) with faster updates, since quicker updates then reach farther routers.
answers.rationale: Update timing does not change the hop count limit that makes distance vector routing unsuitable for networks of this size.

questions.stem: A small IPv4 base network runs RIPv1 and stays well inside the hop count limit. A redesign will give its subnets masks of different lengths, and MSgt Rush wants to keep a simple distance vector protocol. An airman proposes keeping RIPv1 unchanged. Which choice is best supported?

answers.text: Keep RIPv1, since each of its routers can use its own subnet mask.
answers.rationale: RIPv1 updates do not include subnet masks, so all routers must use the same mask; variable length subnet masking is not supported.

answers.text: Move to RIPng, since it is the version developed for IPv6 networks.
answers.rationale: RIPng was developed for IPv6, and this base network uses IPv4 addresses.

answers.text: Move to RIPv2, since it includes subnet mask data in all of its routing updates.
answers.rationale: RIPv1 does not support variable length subnet masking, while RIPv2 allows it by including subnet mask data in all routing updates.

answers.text: Move to Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), since it is also a distance vector protocol.
answers.rationale: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is a link state routing protocol, not the distance vector protocol MSgt Rush wants to keep.

questions.stem: On a network running Routing Information Protocol (RIP), one router begins advertising a wrong route, and soon routers several hops away also list it. An airman says the distant routers must have checked the route against their own maps of the network before accepting it. MSgt Rush must explain how the bad route spread. Which explanation is best supported?

keywords.text: routers several hops away also list it

answers.text: Each router checked it against its own topological map, since Routing Information Protocol (RIP) builds a map of the area.
answers.rationale: Building a complete topological map describes link state routing; Routing Information Protocol (RIP) uses a distance vector algorithm.

answers.text: Each router received it by multicast advertisement, since Routing Information Protocol (RIP) notifies the whole area at once.
answers.rationale: Multicast Link State Advertisements (LSAs) that notify the whole routing area describe link state routing, not the distance vector algorithm that Routing Information Protocol (RIP) uses.

answers.text: Each router copied it from a neighbor's table, since that information cannot be checked for accuracy.
answers.rationale: Routing Information Protocol (RIP) uses a distance vector algorithm, whose routers send their tables to neighbors and build their own tables from them, routing on information that cannot be verified as accurate.

answers.text: Each router learned it from Hello packets, since neighbors exchange routes during discovery.
answers.rationale: Hello packets let network devices identify one another during neighbor discovery; they do not carry routes.

questions.stem: After each link change on a large base network running Routing Information Protocol (RIP), distant routers hold stale routes for a long time. The network must keep growing to a very large size. MSgt Rush wants it to settle on new routes quickly after changes. An airman proposes shortening the RIP update interval. Which choice is best supported?

keywords.text: distant routers hold stale routes for a long time

answers.text: Shorten the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) update interval, since faster updates reach distant routers directly.
answers.rationale: A shorter interval only adds update traffic; Routing Information Protocol (RIP) still has longer convergence times and stays limited by hop count.

answers.text: Move to RIPv2, since it includes subnet mask data in its routing updates.
answers.rationale: RIPv2 improves Routing Information Protocol (RIP), but RIP keeps a hop count metric limited to 15, and hop count limits make distance vector protocols unsuitable for large networks.

answers.text: Add static routes on the distant routers, since they then adjust when the topology changes.
answers.rationale: Static routes do not change until the network administrator changes them, so they would hold stale routes longer.

answers.text: Move to Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), since its Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm allows fast convergence.
answers.rationale: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) uses hierarchical routing that supports very large networks, and its Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm allows fast convergence.

questions.stem: A remote site has a few older routers with little processor power or memory, a small and simple network, and a tight budget for equipment and support. An airman proposes link state routing because it converges faster. MSgt Rush must choose the class of routing algorithm. Which choice is best supported?

answers.text: Link state, since it converges faster and is less prone to routing loops.
answers.rationale: Faster convergence is real, but link state algorithms require more processor power and memory and cost more to implement and support, which these routers and budget lack.

answers.text: Distance vector, since it asks little of the processor and costs less to implement and support.
answers.rationale: Distance vector algorithms are simple, do not require much from the router's processor and are less expensive, while link state algorithms require more processor power and memory.

answers.text: Link state, since it needs less processor power and memory than the other class.
answers.rationale: Link state algorithms require more processor power and memory than the other class, the reverse of this claim.

answers.text: Path vector, since it bases its routing decisions on network policies that administrators set by hand.
answers.rationale: Path vector routing is the exterior gateway approach used between Autonomous Systems (ASs), not a fit for one small site's internal routing.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush is weighing link state against distance vector routing for a base whose links have little spare bandwidth. An airman argues that link state will flood the links, since its updates go to routers throughout the area and not just to neighbors. Which assessment of routine update traffic is best supported?

keywords.text: link state will flood the links

answers.text: Link state uses more, since its updates travel to routers throughout the area.
answers.rationale: Link state updates do reach the whole area, but they are small and sent when link status changes, so routine traffic stays light.

answers.text: Distance vector uses less, since its updates reach the neighboring routers alone.
answers.rationale: Distance vector updates go to neighbors, but they are larger, carry the routing table and are sent at regular intervals as well as for changes.

answers.text: Link state uses less, since its small updates are sent when link status changes.
answers.rationale: Link state algorithms send small updates and only when status changes, while distance vector algorithms send larger updates at regular intervals and for changes.

answers.text: Both use the same, since each sends its whole routing table at regular intervals.
answers.rationale: Link state updates describe a change in link status and are not sent at regular intervals.

questions.stem: Three routers sit in a line on a base network running Routing Information Protocol (RIP): the gate router, a middle router and the hangar router. An airman expects a new route advertised by the gate router to reach the hangar router directly in the gate router's next broadcast update. MSgt Rush must predict how the hangar router learns the route. Which prediction is best supported?

answers.text: The hangar router hears it in the gate router's broadcast, since Routing Information Protocol (RIP) broadcasts cross the Autonomous System (AS).
answers.rationale: A Routing Information Protocol (RIP) broadcast is stopped by the first router interface it meets, so it does not cross the middle router.

answers.text: The hangar router learns it from a Link State Advertisement (LSA), since Routing Information Protocol (RIP) multicasts changes to the area.
answers.rationale: Multicast Link State Advertisements (LSAs) belong to link state routing, not to the distance vector algorithm that Routing Information Protocol (RIP) uses.

answers.text: The hangar router does not learn it, since Routing Information Protocol (RIP) updates stay between directly connected neighbors.
answers.rationale: Updates stay between neighbors, but they pass on one router at a time, so the middle router's own update carries the route onward.

answers.text: The hangar router learns it from the middle router's update, since broadcasts stop at the next router interface.
answers.rationale: Routing Information Protocol (RIP) updates go only to directly connected neighbors and are updated one router at a time, because broadcasts stop at the first router interface.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush is splitting a large Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) network into areas. An airman's design creates two areas joined directly to each other and leaves out Area 0, arguing that the two areas can trade routes between themselves. Which correction is best supported?

answers.text: Keep the two areas joined directly, since each area shares its topology with the other.
answers.rationale: An area's topology is invisible to routers outside the area, so two areas do not trade topology directly.

answers.text: Add an Area 0 backbone joined to both areas, since it distributes routing information between areas.
answers.rationale: The backbone, commonly Area 0, distributes routing information between areas, and it is mandatory and connected to all other areas.

answers.text: Run the Hello protocol between the two areas, since it carries routing information between the areas.
answers.rationale: Hello packets acquire neighbors and act as keep-alives; they do not distribute routing information between areas.

answers.text: Join the areas through an exterior gateway router, since it moves information between areas.
answers.rationale: Exterior gateway routers move information between Autonomous Systems (ASs), and both areas sit inside one autonomous system.

questions.stem: Two Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routers in the same area still show different topology tables well after a link change. An airman says this is normal, since each router keeps its own view of the network. MSgt Rush must judge the claim. Which judgment is best supported?

answers.text: It is normal, since each router builds its topology table from its own links.
answers.rationale: Each router computes its own shortest-path tree, but the topology table holds the advertisements from all routers in the area, so it should match across the area.

answers.text: It is a fault, since routers in one area receive the same advertisements and should match.
answers.rationale: Link State Advertisements (LSAs) notify the other routers in the area, and routers within the same area share the same information, so their topology tables are identical.

answers.text: It is normal, since the tables differ until the next 30-second update.
answers.rationale: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) sends updates when the topology changes, not on a 30-second schedule.

answers.text: It is a fault, since routers in one area should also list the same neighbors in their neighbor tables.
answers.rationale: Each neighbor table records that router's own neighbors, so neighbor tables can differ normally; that is not the mismatch reported here.

questions.stem: A base runs Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) as one very large area, and router processors spike each time the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm runs over the growing topology database. An airman proposes adding memory to every router. MSgt Rush wants to cut the processing load itself. Which change is best supported?

keywords.text: processors spike each time the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm runs

answers.text: Add memory to each router, since the topology database requires considerable memory.
answers.rationale: Memory demand is a separate drawback; the processing load grows with the size of the topology database, which more memory does not shrink.

answers.text: Divide the network into areas, since each topology table holds the advertisements of its own area.
answers.rationale: The algorithm uses more processing power as the topology database grows, and a topology table holds the advertisements from routers in the same area, so smaller areas mean less to process.

answers.text: Move to Routing Information Protocol (RIP), since it keeps no topology database for the algorithm to process.
answers.rationale: Distance vector routing is limited by hop count, which makes it unsuitable for a very large network like this one.

answers.text: Raise the reference bandwidth, since new cost values reduce the algorithm's work.
answers.rationale: The reference bandwidth changes the cost of each interface, not the size of the topology database the algorithm processes.

questions.stem: On an Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) network, the topology table shows both a successor and a feasible successor to a key server network. An airman warns that if the successor link fails, users will lose the server until the whole network recalculates. MSgt Rush must predict the outcome. Which prediction is best supported?

keywords.text: users will lose the server until the whole network recalculates

answers.text: Traffic stops until recalculation, since the routing table holds successor routes alone.
answers.rationale: The routing table is built from successor routes, but when a successor fails the backup already in the topology table moves into the routing table.

answers.text: Traffic shifts to the default route, since that route serves whenever no route to the destination network is known.
answers.rationale: A default route serves when no route is known, and here a backup route to the server is already known.

answers.text: Traffic stops until the next 30-second update, since the routers wait for periodic updates.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) does not make periodic updates; it sends updates when the topology changes.

answers.text: Traffic shifts quickly, since the feasible successor is placed in the routing table when the successor fails.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) converges fast when a feasible successor is available, because that backup route is placed in the routing table when the successor fails.

questions.stem: Reviewing an Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) router, an airman finds a second path to a remote network in the topology table but not in the routing table, and proposes deleting it as a stale entry. MSgt Rush must decide what to do with the entry. Which decision is best supported?

keywords.text: in the topology table but not in the routing table

answers.text: Delete it, since a path that is missing from the routing table is a stale entry.
answers.rationale: The routing table is built from the best paths alone, so a valid backup path stays in the topology table and is not stale.

answers.text: Leave it, since the routing table takes successor routes and the backup stays in the topology table.
answers.rationale: The best paths, successors, are extracted from the topology table to build the routing table, while the backup route, the feasible successor, stays in the topology table.

answers.text: Copy it into the routing table, since the routing table should list both of the known paths to that network.
answers.rationale: The routing table is built from the best path to each network, not from every path the topology table holds.

answers.text: Leave it, since it is a Link State Advertisement (LSA) received from a router in another area.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) has no area concept, and collections of Link State Advertisements (LSAs) belong to Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) topology tables.

questions.stem: A link between two Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) routers keeps dropping and returning, and the router processors spike each time it does. An airman blames the memory needed for the neighbor, topology and routing tables and proposes a memory upgrade. MSgt Rush must name the cause of the spikes. Which cause is best supported?

keywords.text: the router processors spike each time it does

answers.text: The table memory, since Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) needs more memory for its tables.
answers.rationale: Higher memory requirements are a real drawback, but they describe memory use, not processor spikes tied to each drop of the link.

answers.text: The complex routing algorithm, since each drop is a topology change that forces recalculation.
answers.rationale: When a neighbor's hold time expires, the algorithm is informed of the topology change, and the complex algorithm can be processor-intensive during network instability and recalculations.

answers.text: The periodic updates, since Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) sends its full table at intervals.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) does not make periodic updates; it sends updates when the network layout changes.

answers.text: The area databases, since Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) recalculates each area's database.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) has no area concept, so there are no area databases to recalculate.

questions.stem: One router runs Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) for several network protocols and is short on memory, while a similar router running EIGRP for one protocol is not. An airman blames the size of EIGRP's update messages. MSgt Rush must explain the difference. Which explanation is best supported?

keywords.text: for several network protocols and is short on memory

answers.text: Its update messages are larger, since Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) sends full tables on a schedule.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) does not make periodic updates, so scheduled full tables do not explain the memory gap.

answers.text: It keeps a database for each area, since Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) divides the network into areas.
It keeps a separate set of its three tables for each protocol, since those tables drive its memory needs.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) has higher memory requirements for its neighbor, topology and routing tables, and it keeps a separate set for each protocol supported.

answers.text: It runs Dijkstra's algorithm for each protocol, since Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) builds shortest path trees.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) uses the Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL), not Dijkstra's algorithm, so shortest path trees do not explain its memory demand.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush must choose among Routing Information Protocol (RIP), RIPv2, Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGRP) and Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) for a base whose wide area links have little spare bandwidth. An airman favors Routing Information Protocol (RIP) because its updates are simple broadcasts. Which choice is best supported?

keywords.text: wide area links have little spare bandwidth

answers.text: Routing Information Protocol (RIP), since its updates are simple broadcasts to its neighbors.
answers.rationale: Routing Information Protocol (RIP) broadcasts routing updates every 30 seconds as well as when the network layout changes, which keeps putting traffic on the thin links.

answers.text: RIPv2, since it improves on Routing Information Protocol (RIP) by adding subnet mask data to its updates.
answers.rationale: Adding subnet mask data allows variable length subnet masking, but only Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) makes no periodic updates and bounds which routers receive them.

answers.text: Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGRP), since it is the protocol that the newer one was built on.
answers.rationale: Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGRP) consumes significantly more bandwidth than its enhanced successor with bounded, change-driven updates.

answers.text: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP), since it sends bounded updates on topology changes.
answers.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) makes no periodic updates, and its bounded propagation means it consumes significantly less bandwidth than Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGRP) and other distance vector protocols.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush is bringing up Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) between the base and a neighboring Autonomous System (AS). An hour later the two routers still have not formed a session, and an airman suggests waiting longer for Hello packets to discover the neighbor, as Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routers do. Which action is best supported?

keywords.text: still have not formed a session

answers.text: Wait for Hello packets, since routers discover their neighbors through that exchange.
answers.rationale: Hello-based discovery is how interior protocols acquire neighbors; this protocol has no mechanism for automatic neighbor discovery, so waiting changes nothing.

answers.text: Define the neighbor by hand, since Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) has no automatic neighbor discovery.
answers.rationale: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) has no automatic neighbor discovery, so the administrator must define its neighbors and start a Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) session between them.

answers.text: Add a default route, since it sends packets with no known route toward the neighbor.
answers.rationale: A default route sends non-routable packets to one path; it does not create the neighbor relationship the session needs.

answers.text: Enable Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) on the link, since its backbone shares routes between systems.
answers.rationale: The Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) backbone distributes routing information between areas, not between Autonomous Systems (ASs).

questions.stem: Two links join the base to other Autonomous Systems (ASs) through Border Gateway Protocol (BGP): a high-bandwidth link and a slower one. MSgt Rush wants traffic to favor the high-bandwidth link. An airman expects BGP to pick that link on its own by comparing the bandwidth of the two links. Which approach is best supported?

keywords.text: pick that link on its own by comparing the bandwidth

answers.text: Let Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) compare the links, since it measures bandwidth like interior protocols.
answers.rationale: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) does not use metrics such as hop count, bandwidth or delay, so it will not compare the links' bandwidth.

answers.text: Lower the hop count on that link, since Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) chooses the path with fewer hops.
answers.rationale: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) does not use hop count as a metric, so changing hops does not steer its choice.

answers.text: Add a feasible successor, since Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) keeps a backup route in its topology table.
answers.rationale: Feasible successors are the backup routes in Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) topology tables, not a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) tool.

answers.text: Set a policy favoring that link, since Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routes by administrator-entered policies.
answers.rationale: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) makes routing decisions from network policies that administrators enter, and its path attributes are manually inserted into the BGP process.

questions.stem: While reading an older routing manual, an airman sees the routers between base subnets called gateways and concludes that each one must convert traffic from one protocol format to another. MSgt Rush must correct the reading before the airman relabels the network documentation. Which correction is best supported?

keywords.text: concludes that each one must convert traffic

answers.text: Gateway names a protocol converter, so those devices translate between formats.
answers.rationale: Converting between protocols or formats is what the term often means in today's terminology, not what it meant in older routing usage.

answers.text: Gateway meant a router in older usage, so those devices route packets between networks.
answers.rationale: Routing devices have traditionally been called gateways, meaning dedicated routers that send packets between subnets and networks, while the converter meaning is today's usage.

answers.text: Gateway names a switch, so those devices move frames by reading hardware addresses.
