Classful routing makes every router in the network use the same subnet mask; it does not combine networks.
A Variable Length Subnet Mask (VLSM) means one network is assigned more than one subnet mask; it does not combine networks.

questions.stem: The squadron's headquarters subnet needs many hosts while each shop subnet needs only a few. What does a Variable Length Subnet Mask (VLSM) reduce here?

keywords.text: needs many hosts while each shop subnet needs only a few

answers.rationale: Letting each subnet have a different number of hosts, as a Variable Length Subnet Mask (VLSM) does, reduces the number of wasted addresses.
A Variable Length Subnet Mask (VLSM) means the network is assigned more than one subnet mask, so masks are not reduced.
A Variable Length Subnet Mask (VLSM) is used when subnetting a subnet, which breaks subnets into further subnets.
Each switch port is a collision domain because it shares no bandwidth, which has nothing to do with address use.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush has settled how many subnets a new squadron building will have. What else does his simple network design rest on?

answers.rationale: A simple network design is based on how many subnets are needed and how many hosts are needed for the subnet.
Supernets aggregate networks into larger ones; a simple network design is based on two other things.
Trunk links are not one of the two things a simple network design is based on.
Server counts are not one of the two things a simple network design is based on.

questions.stem: An airman must connect a new patch cable to the exact switch interface MSgt Rush planned. Which detail on the physical network diagram shows where it goes?

answers.rationale: A cable category, such as CAT5e or CAT 6, tells which twisted pair cable to use, not where it plugs in.
Drawings may label port numbers so the airman knows which port to plug the cable in.
Connector types, such as RJ45 or RS232, tell which connector a cable needs, not where it plugs in.
Single mode or multimode tells which fiber optic cable to install, not where it plugs in.

questions.stem: An airman's plan joins a star-wired office to a full mesh of core routers. Which topology name belongs on the plan?

answers.rationale: A tree topology joins star-configured segments to a linear bus backbone, and this plan has no bus.
A star topology describes the office alone, not its join to a full mesh core.
A full mesh topology describes the core routers alone, not the star-wired office joined to them.
Any combination of topologies other than bus and star is a hybrid topology.

questions.stem: An airman's drawing shows how Ethernet moves data between the nodes of an office network. Which topology does the drawing document?

keywords.text: how Ethernet moves data between the nodes

answers.rationale: Physical topology is the physical interconnection of network devices, not how a protocol moves data between nodes.
Logical topology is bound to network protocols such as Ethernet and describes how data moves through the network.
A hybrid topology is a combination of physical topologies, not a view bound to a protocol.
A full mesh topology connects each node directly to every other node, a physical layout rather than a protocol view.

questions.stem: On a data flow diagram of the squadron supply system, an airman must draw the archive where inventory records rest between transactions. Which symbol does it need?

keywords.text: archive where inventory records rest between transactions

answers.rationale: Data stores are data repositories for data that is not moving, like records at rest in an archive.
Data flows show movement of data in the system, not records at rest in an archive.
Processes transform incoming data flows to outgoing data flows; they do not hold records at rest.
External entities are sources or destinations outside the system boundary, not an archive inside the system.

questions.stem: A laptop shares resources with other computers. What role is it performing?

answers.rationale: A client initiates contact to use a shared resource, not to provide one.
A thin client relies on another computer for most of its work, so it uses resources rather than sharing its own.
A domain controller manages Active Directory (AD) resource information; sharing resources alone does not make one.

questions.reviewCue: This role is a job any device can do, not a particular shape of computer.

questions.stem: One server handles both printing and website hosting for an office. What type of server is it?

answers.rationale: A single-purpose server is committed to one specific task, not several.
A multi-purpose server performs multiple functions, such as printing and website hosting.
A web server is dedicated to serving up web pages and nothing else.
A print server is dedicated to facilitating printing and nothing else.

questions.reviewCue: Picture one machine wearing several hats at the same time.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a peer-to-peer network?

answers.text: Clients send requests through a server
answers.rationale: In a client-server network, clients send requests to a server and use it as an intermediary, while peers communicate directly.

answers.text: A central database authenticates each user
answers.rationale: A central database of account and security information that authenticates users belongs to a domain, while peer-to-peer management is decentralized.

answers.text: No computer has more authority than another
answers.rationale: By default, no computer on a peer-to-peer network has more authority than any other, and there are no dedicated servers.

answers.text: Servers have more processing power than clients
answers.rationale: Servers with more processing power than clients belong to a client-server network, while a peer-to-peer network has no dedicated servers.

questions.reviewCue: Picture teammates sharing directly, with no dedicated team captain.

questions.stem: A device requests a shared resource from a server. What role is it performing?

answers.rationale: Servers provide shared resources to other computers; this device is asking for one.
A client initiates contact with a server to use a shareable resource.
A domain controller manages Active Directory (AD) information; requesting a shared resource does not make a device one.
A web server provides website data to browsers; it supplies content rather than requesting a resource.

questions.reviewCue: At a service counter, this role is the one asking for something.

questions.stem: A workstation loses its network connection. Which statement is true?

answers.text: It stops working until the network returns
answers.rationale: Clients that cannot function until the server is restored depend on a server; workstations do not.

answers.text: It needs a terminal server to run applications
answers.rationale: Terminal servers supply applications to remote clients; a workstation has its own software.

answers.text: It can function using its own hardware and software
answers.rationale: A workstation has all essential hardware and software to function without a network.

answers.text: It needs a server to do its processing
answers.rationale: Relying on another computer for most work describes a thin client.

questions.reviewCue: Losing the network is like losing delivery service; you can still use what is already at home.

questions.stem: Which device relies on a central server for most applications, processing and memory?

answers.rationale: A thick client has local applications and can function independently of the server.
A terminal server is the server that supplies applications to remote clients, not the device that relies on one.
A workstation can function completely independently of a server or network.

questions.reviewCue: This client travels light because the server carries most of the workload.

questions.stem: Which device runs locally installed applications and only occasionally needs to connect to the central server?

answers.rationale: A terminal server supplies applications to remote clients; it is a server, not a device running its own installed applications.
A thick client runs local applications and does not always need a server connection.
An application server provides services to other software; it is a server, not a device that runs local applications.

questions.reviewCue: Picture a field kit that carries its own tools and checks in with headquarters now and then.

questions.stem: Why is a client-server network easier to organize and back up than a peer-to-peer network?

keywords.text: easier to organize and back up

answers.rationale: Equal authority describes peer-to-peer networks, where decentralized management makes resources harder to organize.

answers.text: Each computer manages its own resources
answers.rationale: Each computer controlling its own shared files is a decentralized workgroup, which makes backups harder to organize.

answers.text: Clients share resources directly with each other
answers.rationale: Client-server clients do not share directly; they use the server as an intermediary.

answers.text: Resources are hosted on a central server
answers.rationale: One server hosts the resources, giving a centralized data source for updates and backups.

questions.reviewCue: One shared supply room is easier to organize than supplies scattered across every desk.

questions.stem: What makes client-server networks more expensive to set up and maintain?

answers.text: Added server workload from more clients
answers.rationale: More clients slow the network through server workload; this is not the setup cost.
Specialized server equipment and software add to setup and maintenance costs.
A server failure is a reliability drawback, not the reason for higher costs.
Central management is a client-server advantage, not a cost.

questions.reviewCue: A dedicated service counter needs its own purpose-built tools and upkeep before it can serve anyone.

questions.stem: When the central server goes down, clients cannot function until it is restored. Which client-server disadvantage is this?

answers.rationale: The network relies on the central server, so losing it stops clients from working.
Higher setup and maintenance cost is a client-server disadvantage, but it does not stop clients when the server goes down.
Added clients can slow the network, but that does not stop clients until a restore.
Data loss is a client-server disadvantage only when a crashed server holds the only copy and no backup exists; clients stopping is the failure point.

questions.reviewCue: Picture a bridge resting on one support beam: if that beam breaks, nobody crosses.

questions.stem: Which arrangement lets each computer control its own shared resources?

answers.rationale: A domain manages access centrally through shared account and security information, not on each computer.
In a workgroup, each computer controls access to its own shared resources.
An Organizational Unit (OU) is a container inside a domain for users, computers and groups; it does not leave control to each computer.
A site describes a physical network location by its subnets; it does not decide who controls shared resources.

questions.reviewCue: Think of neighbors who each decide who may borrow their tools.

questions.stem: Which arrangement uses centralized authentication to control access to network resources?

answers.rationale: In a workgroup, each computer controls access to its own resources, so there is no centralized authentication.
An Organizational Unit (OU) groups users, computers and groups for organization; it does not itself provide authentication.
A domain provides central authentication and control of network access.
A site maps a physical location by its subnets; it does not authenticate users or control access.

questions.reviewCue: Picture a workplace with a central badge desk that controls network access.

questions.stem: Which server role manages resource information in Active Directory (AD)?

answers.rationale: A mail server transfers email with a mail-transfer protocol; it does not manage directory information.
A domain controller stores and manages Active Directory (AD) information.
An audio/video server streams and broadcasts multimedia; it keeps no Active Directory (AD) information.
A File Transfer Protocol (FTP) server moves files between computers; it does not manage Active Directory (AD) information.

questions.reviewCue: When a user account changes, consider which server maintains the shared directory record.

questions.stem: Which server is sometimes called a type of middleware and often connects end users with database servers?

answers.rationale: A Domain Name System (DNS) server translates names into addresses; it is not middleware between users and databases.
A Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server assigns addresses to devices; it does not connect users with database servers.
Application servers are sometimes called a type of middleware and provide services beyond those available from the Operating System (OS).
A proxy mediates between a client and an external server, not between end users and database servers.

questions.reviewCue: Like a kitchen between diners and the pantry: it turns stored ingredients into the dishes diners order.

questions.stem: Which server role provides multimedia streaming and broadcasting to users?

answers.rationale: An audio/video server provides streaming and broadcasting services.
A mail server transfers email between systems; it does not stream or broadcast multimedia.
A Domain Name System (DNS) server translates host names into addresses; it does not stream multimedia.
A Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server assigns addresses to devices; it does not broadcast media to users.

questions.reviewCue: Think of a booth that sends a live event out to an audience as it happens.

questions.stem: Which description fits a cloud server?

answers.rationale: Functioning without a network describes a workstation.

answers.text: Pooled resources delivered over a network
answers.rationale: Cloud servers provide pooled, centralized, virtualized resources delivered over a network, typically the Internet.

answers.text: A terminal with little or no storage
answers.rationale: A desktop terminal with a small or no hard drive describes a thin client.

answers.text: One server dedicated to one task
answers.rationale: A server dedicated to one task describes a single-purpose server.

questions.reviewCue: Think of computing capacity supplied remotely, like a utility rather than equipment at your desk.

questions.stem: Which server automatically assigns each computer an Internet Protocol (IP) address from a list of available addresses?

keywords.text: assigns each computer an Internet Protocol (IP) address

answers.rationale: A Domain Name System (DNS) server translates host names into addresses; it does not assign addresses to computers.
A proxy passes requests between a client and an external server; it does not assign addresses.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically assigns Internet Protocol (IP) addresses from a list of available addresses.
A web server delivers website data to browsers; it does not give computers their addresses.

questions.reviewCue: Picture an address checkout desk that hands out an available address.

questions.stem: Which server translates a host name into an Internet Protocol (IP) address?

keywords.text: host name into an Internet Protocol (IP) address

answers.rationale: A Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server assigns addresses to computers; it does not translate host names.
A mail server transfers email; it does not look up the address for a host name.
A File Transfer Protocol (FTP) server moves files between computers; it does not translate host names into addresses.
Domain Name System (DNS) translates host names into Internet Protocol (IP) addresses.

questions.reviewCue: Picture the network's contact list: look up a person and get their number.

questions.stem: Which server acts as an intermediary between a client and an external server?

answers.rationale: A Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server assigns addresses; it does not stand between a client and an external server.
A proxy passes requests between clients and external servers.
A mail server transfers email for its users; it does not stand between a client and an external server.
An audio/video server streams its own multimedia to users; it is not an intermediary for other servers.

questions.reviewCue: Picture a receptionist passing your request onward and returning the reply.

questions.stem: Besides mediating requests, what can a proxy server do for devices on an internal network?

answers.text: Assign them Internet Protocol (IP) addresses automatically
answers.rationale: Automatically assigning Internet Protocol (IP) addresses is a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server task.

answers.text: Translate their domain names into Internet Protocol (IP) addresses
answers.rationale: Translating domain names to Internet Protocol (IP) addresses is a Domain Name System (DNS) server task.

answers.text: Hide their Internet Protocol (IP) addresses from the Internet
answers.rationale: Proxy servers can hide the addresses of all devices on the network from the Internet.

answers.text: Move one or more files between computers
answers.rationale: Moving files between computers is a File Transfer Protocol (FTP) server task.

questions.reviewCue: Picture sending a letter through a forwarding office so the recipient never sees where you live.

questions.stem: What does Telnet let a user do on a remote computer?

answers.rationale: Assigning addresses from an available list is a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server task.
Telnet enables users to remotely log on to a host computer and execute tasks.
Web servers store, process and transfer website data.
Audio/video servers provide multimedia streaming and broadcasting.

questions.reviewCue: Picture sitting at your own desk while typing commands on a computer in another building.

questions.stem: A server uses Remote Desktop Services to provide applications to remote users. What role is it performing?

answers.rationale: A mail server transfers email; it does not supply applications to remote users.
A Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server assigns addresses; it does not run Remote Desktop Services for remote users.
A server running Remote Desktop Services acts as a terminal server, supplying applications and resources to remote clients.
A Domain Name System (DNS) server translates names into addresses; it does not provide applications to remote users.

questions.reviewCue: Like a shared workshop whose tools never leave the building, while many members work with them from far away.

questions.stem: Which server type recreates a physical server in software and allows its resources to be reassigned?

keywords.text: recreates a physical server in software

answers.rationale: A virtual server recreates physical-server functions, making resources easier to reassign.
Cloud servers pool virtualized resources and deliver them over a network; that remote delivery, not the software recreation, defines them.
Terminal servers provide applications and resources to multiple remote users.
Application servers provide application services and can act as middleware.

questions.reviewCue: Imagine moving a server's assigned resources without moving a physical chassis.

questions.stem: Which server stores and transfers the pages a browser requests using Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)?

answers.rationale: A mail server transfers email with a mail-transfer protocol, not pages to a browser.
A web server stores and delivers website content to browsers.
A Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server assigns addresses to computers; it does not deliver pages to browsers.
Telnet servers let users log on remotely and execute tasks; they do not deliver pages to browsers.

questions.stem: Maintainers rotate among shop-floor desktops each shift. Each desktop already runs the needed applications locally, but users lose their personal settings and data when they change machines. MSgt Rush rules out new desktop Virtual Machines (VMs) and server-side application processing. Which approach best fits?

answers.text: Pool the desktops' drives into one logical storage device managed centrally.
answers.rationale: Storage pooling combines devices into one logical store; it does not load each user's settings at sign-in.

answers.text: Deliver each user's desktop from a shared server through presentation sessions.
answers.rationale: Presentation virtualization processes applications on the server, which MSgt Rush ruled out.

answers.text: Store each user's profile centrally and load it on the current desktop.
answers.rationale: Profile virtualization keeps user data centrally and loads it to each maintainer's current client device.

answers.text: Give each maintainer a dedicated virtual desktop through Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI).
answers.rationale: Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) creates a Virtual Machine (VM) for each client, which MSgt Rush ruled out.

questions.stem: Field laptops on a slow network link need a large mapping program, but users touch a small set of its features. The program must still run on each laptop's own processor, and administrators do not want a complete installation on every machine. Which delivery approach best fits these constraints?

keywords.text: touch a small set of its features

answers.text: Presentation virtualization, sending each laptop a picture of the running program.
answers.rationale: With presentation virtualization, applications are not processed on the client, which the program requires.

answers.text: Copy the complete installer to each laptop from a file server.
answers.rationale: A complete installation on each machine is what administrators want to avoid.

answers.text: Hardware emulation, presenting a simulated device on which the program runs.
answers.rationale: Emulating hardware changes what a guest sees, not how a program is delivered.

answers.text: Application streaming, sending the program's portions to the laptop when required.
answers.rationale: Streaming avoids a full install by offering needed portions across the network for the device to use.

questions.stem: A platform team runs four Linux applications and one Windows-only application, each in its own Virtual Machine (VM) on a Linux host. To save resources and start workloads faster, the team proposes moving the five applications into containers on that same host. Which assessment is best supported?

answers.text: The Linux applications can move; the Windows application cannot use the Linux host's kernel.
answers.rationale: Containers share the host Operating System (OS) kernel, so applications must be compatible with that host OS.

answers.text: The five can move, since each container carries its own guest Operating System (OS).
answers.rationale: Containers share the host's kernel instead of replicating an Operating System (OS) for each application.

answers.text: The Windows application can move; the Linux applications each need a guest Operating System (OS) on the host.
answers.rationale: Containers on a Linux host share its kernel instead of giving each application its own guest Operating System (OS).

answers.text: The five can move, but each container will be larger than its Virtual Machine (VM).
answers.rationale: Containers are much smaller than Virtual Machines (VMs) and still must match the host Operating System (OS).

questions.stem: A server team compares two designs for one Virtual Machine (VM). In Design X, the guest Operating System (OS) is unchanged and the hypervisor presents a simulated switch to it. In Design Y, the guest kernel is edited so the guest talks directly to the host through the hypervisor. Which evaluation is accurate?

answers.text: Design X is paravirtualization, since the hypervisor communicates for the guest.
answers.rationale: An unchanged guest using a simulated device describes hardware emulation.

answers.text: Design Y is paravirtualization, since its guest makes calls through the hypervisor.
answers.rationale: A modified guest kernel making hyper calls through the hypervisor streamlines communication and increases processing.

answers.text: Design Y is hardware emulation, since the guest reaches the host directly.
answers.rationale: Emulation presents a simulated device to the guest; it does not require editing the guest kernel.

answers.text: Design Y is a container, since the guest shares the host's kernel.
answers.rationale: Design Y modifies the guest's own kernel; containers share the host kernel without a guest Operating System (OS).

questions.stem: Proposal 1 presents several network storage arrays as a single device managed from one console. Proposal 2 points virtualization software at a Virtual Machine (VM) image and lets the software decide which physical server runs it. MSgt Rush says both are server consolidation because both reduce administration. Which evaluation is accurate?

answers.text: Both are storage virtualization, since each hides physical hardware behind software.
answers.rationale: Proposal 2 selects a host for a Virtual Machine (VM); it does not pool storage devices.

answers.text: MSgt Rush is right, since both cut the number of servers to maintain.
answers.rationale: Consolidation reduces physical servers; neither proposal removes servers.

answers.text: Proposal 1 is server pooling; Proposal 2 is load balancing across hardware.
answers.rationale: Pooling selects hosts for Virtual Machines (VMs), and load balancing divides workload among VMs on separate hardware.

answers.text: Proposal 1 is storage virtualization; Proposal 2 is server pooling.
answers.rationale: One pools storage into a single logical device; the other lets software pick the best physical server.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush wants airmen in a lab class to reproduce a suspected configuration defect on a copy of a multi-server network without touching the live network. After each lab, every airman's machine must return to its exact pre-lab state for the next class. Which plan meets both needs?

answers.text: Build a virtual sandbox of the systems and take a snapshot before each lab.
answers.rationale: Sandboxes allow troubleshooting without harming a live network, and snapshots copy a Virtual Machine (VM) at a point in time.

answers.text: Run the lab Virtual Machines (VMs) on two hosts with load balancing so one failure causes no outage.
answers.rationale: Load balancing protects against a single point of failure; it neither isolates the lab nor restores machines.

answers.text: Use server pooling on production hosts so software picks a server for each lab.
answers.rationale: Pooling chooses a host for each Virtual Machine (VM); using production hosts does not keep the lab off the live network.

answers.text: Use profile virtualization so each airman's settings reload in the next class.
answers.rationale: Profiles carry user data, not the full machine state needed for an exact restore.

questions.stem: A wing proposes three actions: (1) move 12 underused physical servers onto 2 hosts as Virtual Machines (VMs); (2) run the same application in virtual machines on two separate hosts so losing one host causes no outage; (3) let software pick the physical server for each new VM image. Which mapping is correct, in order?

answers.text: Server pooling, load balancing and server consolidation.
answers.rationale: Action 1 reduces the number of physical servers, which is not what pooling does.

answers.text: Server consolidation, load balancing and server pooling.
answers.rationale: Fewer physical servers, workload split across hardware and software host selection match the three actions.

answers.text: Load balancing, server pooling and server consolidation.
answers.rationale: Each action is matched to another action's technique.

answers.text: Server consolidation, Disaster Recovery (DR) and load balancing.
answers.rationale: Disaster Recovery (DR) addresses losses far worse than one failed host, which is all action 2 describes.

questions.stem: A recovery plan copies Virtual Machine (VM) image files each night to a site 200 miles away in case the main data center is lost. The remote site has storage for the files and nothing else installed. Leadership asks whether services could restart there after a data-center loss. Which assessment is best supported?

answers.text: Yes; the copied image files can start themselves once the remote storage is online.
answers.rationale: Image files are data on storage; they cannot start themselves, and the remote site has nothing else installed.

answers.text: Not yet; the images must first be copied back to the main data center.
answers.rationale: The plan exists for losing the main data center, so recovery cannot depend on copying the images back there.

answers.text: Not yet; a hypervisor on host hardware must be in place to start the images.
answers.rationale: Image files support recovery when a hypervisor on a host providing processing and memory can start them.

answers.text: No; virtualization suits single-Virtual Machine (VM) crashes, not losing an entire data center.
answers.rationale: Virtualization is an ideal technology for Disaster Recovery (DR), including a lost data center.

questions.stem: An airman drafts a small change to a virtual host's network settings, and the review board approves it. The next approved change-control window opens tonight at 2200, but the staging security tests are not booked until tomorrow. MSgt Rush says the change is tiny and already approved, so it can go in tonight. Which plan best follows change-control guidance?

keywords.text: staging security tests are not booked until tomorrow

answers.text: Apply it in tonight's approved window, since board approval stands in for staging tests.
answers.rationale: Approval does not replace testing; a change is tested in staging before it goes into an approved window.

answers.text: Run the staging tests tomorrow and apply the change as soon as they pass.
answers.rationale: Once testing is complete, changes are made during approved change-control windows, not as soon as tests pass.

answers.text: Apply it tonight, then run the staging tests to confirm nothing broke.
answers.rationale: Staging tests come first, to show the change does not adversely affect the host or guest Operating Systems (OSs).

answers.text: Test it in staging tomorrow, then apply it in the first approved window after that.
answers.rationale: Changes are tested in staging first and then made only in approved windows, however trivial they appear, so tonight comes too early.

questions.stem: An audit finds guest Operating Systems (OSs) and the web and database servers fully patched. Nobody checked the host OS, the hypervisor, the Virtual Machine (VM) management software, an open-source library or the workstation software used to run VMs. Which remediation best closes the gap?

answers.text: Bring the overlooked infrastructure and smaller components into the routine patch cycle.
answers.rationale: Host, guest, virtualization and management software and Virtual Machine (VM)-running workstation software all need patches.

answers.text: Keep patching the guests, since the hypervisor isolates them from host flaws.
answers.rationale: The host and virtualization software must be patched as well as the guests.

answers.text: Patch the hypervisor and host Operating System (OS), leaving the library and workstation software for later.
answers.rationale: Small third-party and open-source components are commonly forgotten and can expose critical issues.

answers.text: Take snapshots of each guest so unpatched components can be rolled back.
answers.rationale: A snapshot copies a Virtual Machine (VM) at a point in time; it does not patch any component.

questions.stem: An airman downloads a free, preconfigured firewall virtual appliance from a vendor and plans to clone it onto hosts at five sites this week. Unit rules forbid connecting unapproved physical hardware to the network, and the airman argues those rules do not cover a downloaded Virtual Machine (VM). MSgt Rush must set the conditions for the rollout. Which plan best addresses the risks?

keywords.text: clone it onto hosts at five sites

answers.text: Deploy the clones, then snapshot each one so it can be restored if problems appear.
answers.rationale: A point-in-time copy neither controls the appliance's contents nor keeps track of the new machines.

answers.text: Approve its contents under the hardware rules, then record each clone and its licenses in an inventory.
answers.rationale: Appliance contents need rules like those for unapproved hardware, and machines spun up from clones need inventory so systems and licenses are not lost.

answers.text: Approve its contents under the hardware rules once; its clones then need no further records.
answers.rationale: Clones spun up on the fly create asset-tracking gaps, so new machines and their licenses still need an inventory.

answers.text: Record each clone and its licenses in an inventory; tracking the copies controls what they contain.
answers.rationale: An inventory tracks machines but does not control the appliance's contents, which need approval like physical hardware.

questions.stem: A team gives each airman who administers its systems an individual account inside every guest Virtual Machine (VM), linked to Active Directory (AD). The host, however, is managed through one shared local account whose password every airman on the team knows. Which assessment identifies the main remaining weakness and its fix?

answers.text: The shared host account is acceptable, since guest accounts already trace each airman.
answers.rationale: Host access is a powerful privilege over guests, so tracing guest logons leaves host actions untraced.

answers.text: Guest controls are enough, since each guest has its own Operating System (OS).
answers.rationale: Separate guest systems do not limit the host account's power over them.

answers.text: Tie host sign-ins to identity solutions and defined roles, since host access outranks guests.
answers.rationale: Host authentication should link to existing identity solutions, with responsibilities assigned to defined roles.

answers.text: Rotate the shared password monthly, keeping one host account for the team.
answers.rationale: A rotated shared password still does not tie host actions to individuals through identity management.

questions.stem: A virtualization team archives logs for the required three years and feeds them to the network's event notification system. Administrators can edit log files, and nobody is assigned to watch alerts. Last month, no one could tell who powered off a web server Virtual Machine (VM). Which improvement best addresses the causes?

keywords.text: who powered off a web server Virtual Machine (VM)

answers.text: Extend log retention to five years so the audit trail covers more history.
answers.rationale: Longer retention neither stops log tampering nor gets alerts watched.

answers.text: Replace the event notification feed with the vendor's built-in audit trail.
answers.rationale: Built-in audit trails should be integrated with event notification systems, not substituted for them.

answers.text: Take regular snapshots of the web server Virtual Machine (VM) so its power state can be restored.
answers.rationale: Restoring a Virtual Machine (VM) does not show who powered it off or protect the logs.

answers.text: Restrict who can change logs and have staff monitor and respond.
answers.rationale: Logs need access controls against tampering, and logging is only useful if staff monitor and respond.

questions.stem: A virtual estate has grown to 300 Virtual Machines (VMs). Administrators no longer know what many of them do, storage and bandwidth are running short, and license counts no longer match deployed software. A proposal would delete this week each VM that nobody recognizes. Which approach best addresses both the sprawl and the licensing risk?

keywords.text: delete this week each VM that nobody recognizes

answers.text: Inventory Virtual Machines (VMs) and software, confirm each VM's function, then retire and audit.
answers.rationale: Detailed inventories counter sprawl and licensing risk, and confirming function avoids deleting a needed Virtual Machine (VM).

answers.text: Delete unrecognized Virtual Machines (VMs) now, then audit licenses against the VMs left.
answers.rationale: Deleting a Virtual Machine (VM) without knowing its function can be disastrous.

answers.text: Add server pooling so software tracks which host runs each Virtual Machine (VM).
answers.rationale: Pooling selects hosts for Virtual Machines (VMs); it does not rebuild software or license inventories.

answers.text: Consolidate the Virtual Machines (VMs) onto fewer hosts to cut power and maintenance costs.
answers.rationale: Consolidation reduces physical servers but leaves unknown Virtual Machines (VMs) and license gaps in place.

questions.stem: Two candidate hosts are offered for a project whose Virtual Machine (VM) list is not final. Host X has large disk capacity but modest processing and memory; Host Y has strong processing and memory but modest disk. An airman wants Host X now because VM files take space. Which planning step is best?

answers.text: Choose Host X, since storage limits how many Virtual Machines (VMs) a host can store.
answers.rationale: Storage matters, but processing and memory are the main limits, and needs depend on the Virtual Machines (VMs).

answers.text: First set the number and roles of the Virtual Machines (VMs), then size the host.
answers.rationale: Host requirements depend on the number and roles of the Virtual Machines (VMs) it will manage.

answers.text: Choose Host Y, since processing and memory are the main limits on Virtual Machine (VM) count.
answers.rationale: Storage still limits Virtual Machine (VM) count, and the unfinished VM list leaves the needs unknown.

answers.text: Choose either host, since hypervisors can reallocate memory to cover a shortfall.
answers.rationale: Reallocation shares a host's existing resources; it cannot add capacity the host lacks.

questions.stem: A proposed hypervisor update could let some users see records above their access level, could corrupt a shared database, and needs a reboot that halts the payroll Virtual Machine (VM) for an hour. MSgt Rush's checklist asks whether the update installs cleanly. Which mapping of each risk to the security fundamental it affects should the change review use?

answers.text: Exposure: integrity; corruption: confidentiality; reboot: availability.
answers.rationale: Seeing records above an access level changes none of them, so it is not an integrity risk.

answers.text: Exposure: confidentiality; corruption: availability; reboot: integrity.
answers.rationale: A reboot that halts the payroll Virtual Machine (VM) changes no records, so it is not an integrity risk.

answers.text: Exposure: confidentiality; corruption: integrity; reboot: availability.
answers.rationale: Seeing records above an access level breaks confidentiality, corrupting data breaks integrity, and halting a needed machine breaks availability; one change can affect all three.

answers.text: Exposure: availability; corruption: integrity; reboot: confidentiality.
answers.rationale: A reboot that halts the payroll Virtual Machine (VM) exposes no records, so it is not a confidentiality risk.

questions.stem: A wing keeps its accounts in one domain, and users find resources by name. One squadron moves to a building on a new Internet Protocol (IP) subnet range across a Wide Area Network (WAN) link, and its users still need the same resources. MSgt Rush must decide what the directory design should change for the move. Which assessment fits the stated design?

keywords.text: a new Internet Protocol (IP) subnet range

answers.text: Model the new subnet range as a site, since one domain can span several sites.
answers.rationale: Sites map the physical network as Internet Protocol (IP) subnet ranges, and two sites on different networks can belong to the same domain.

answers.text: Create a new domain for the building, since a domain is defined by its subnet range.
answers.rationale: A domain groups resources logically so users find them by name; it is not defined by a subnet range.

answers.text: Create a separate forest, since a Wide Area Network (WAN) link between buildings splits the directory boundary.
answers.rationale: A forest is the outermost directory boundary; a Wide Area Network (WAN) link between buildings does not split it.

answers.text: Change the schema, since the moved accounts now need a different set of object classes.
answers.rationale: The schema holds class and attribute definitions; moving users to a new subnet does not change their object class.

questions.stem: During a domain controller rebuild, MSgt Rush sorts three data sets that the server holds: settings objects that apply across the entire forest, the class and attribute rules that any new printer object has to follow, and the account records for one domain's users, computers and groups. Which partition assignment, in that order, matches the three data sets?

keywords.text: settings objects that apply across the entire forest

answers.text: Global catalog, site, and Organizational Unit (OU), respectively.
answers.rationale: A global catalog, a site and an Organizational Unit (OU) are not directory partitions, so none of them is the storage asked for.

answers.text: Configuration partition, schema, and domain partition, respectively.
answers.rationale: Forest-wide settings, class and attribute definitions, and one domain's users, computers and groups are stored in these three partitions.

answers.text: Domain partition, configuration partition, and schema, respectively.
answers.rationale: This puts forest-wide settings in per-domain storage and puts domain accounts with the definitions of object classes.

answers.text: Schema, domain partition, and configuration partition, respectively.
answers.rationale: This stores forest-wide settings with class definitions and stores one domain's accounts as forest-wide settings.

questions.stem: An application team asks for a new kind of directory entry, a badge reader, with fields that no existing type offers. The same week, the help desk updates the phone number on an existing user account. MSgt Rush wants to route each request to the right approver and must explain the difference between them. Which distinction should guide the routing?

keywords.text: a new kind of directory entry

answers.text: Both requests change the schema, since both store new information in the directory.
answers.rationale: A phone number change edits data on one existing object and leaves class and attribute definitions alone.

answers.text: The first changes an attribute value; the second defines a new object class.
answers.rationale: This reverses the two: a new entry type with new fields is a definition change, while the phone update is object data.

answers.text: The first changes schema definitions; the second changes one object's attribute value.
answers.rationale: A new class with new fields alters class and attribute definitions, while a phone number is an attribute value on one user object.

answers.text: Both requests change individual objects, so neither one affects class definitions.
answers.rationale: A new kind of entry with new fields needs a definition for that class, not just data on an existing object.

questions.stem: The medical group help desk needs to reset passwords for its own staff, who work in two buildings on different subnets. It must not gain rights over Finance accounts in the same domain, and the wing will not restructure its domains. The wing wants one place to grant this right. Which design meets these conditions?

keywords.text: one place to grant this right

answers.text: Define a site for each building and grant the help desk rights on each site.
answers.rationale: Sites map the physical network by subnet; they split the staff across two places and are not administrative containers.

answers.text: Add the help desk to the domain's Access Control List (ACL) so it can manage domain user accounts.
answers.rationale: Domain-wide access entries would reach the Finance accounts that the help desk must not control.

answers.text: Create a child domain for the medical group and manage its accounts from there.
answers.rationale: A new child domain restructures the domains, which the wing has ruled out.

answers.text: Place the staff accounts in one Organizational Unit (OU) and delegate through its Access Control List (ACL).
answers.rationale: An Organizational Unit (OU) groups users, and modifying its Access Control List (ACL) delegates control of only that unit's objects.

questions.stem: A base directory has AF.Domain with child domains such as 81Wing.AF.Domain, and a separate Medical.Domain with its own child domain, Surgery.Medical.Domain. Each structure keeps its own naming pattern, yet both share one global catalog and one directory schema. A briefing slide must label the two levels of grouping. Which labeling is correct?

keywords.text: share one global catalog and one directory schema

answers.text: Each naming structure is a domain tree; the two together form a forest.
answers.rationale: Domains sharing a namespace form a tree, and trees sharing a global catalog and schema form a forest.

answers.text: Each naming structure is a forest; the two together form a domain tree.
answers.rationale: This reverses the levels: the two structures do not share one namespace, but they do share a catalog and schema.

answers.text: Each naming structure is an Organizational Unit (OU); the two together form one domain.
answers.rationale: These structures are made of separate domains, while an Organizational Unit (OU) is a subdivision within one domain.

answers.text: Each naming structure is a site; the two together form one domain.
answers.rationale: Sites map the physical network as subnet ranges, and the scenario describes only naming and shared directory data.

questions.stem: During a new deployment, the team builds AF.Domain first and later adds 81Wing.AF.Domain beneath it. A year later, a third domain, 403Wing.AF.Domain, is added beneath AF.Domain as well. A deployment checklist asks the team to record the role of each of the three domains. Which description is correct?

answers.text: The three are Organizational Units (OUs), since they share the AF.Domain naming pattern.
answers.rationale: These are separate domains; an Organizational Unit (OU) is a subdivision placed within a domain.

answers.text: AF.Domain is the forest root, since it was built first; the other two are its child domains.
answers.rationale: The first domain created is the forest root, and domains that branch from that root are child domains.

answers.text: 403Wing.AF.Domain becomes the forest root, since it is the newest domain added.
answers.rationale: The forest root role follows the first domain created, not the most recent one.

answers.text: 81Wing.AF.Domain is the forest root, since it was the first domain beneath AF.Domain.
answers.rationale: The forest root is the first domain created in the forest, and 81Wing was built after AF.Domain.

questions.stem: A help desk tool at the 81st Wing must locate a printer published in the Medical.Domain tree, which is in the same forest. MSgt Rush's replacement tool searches only the domain partition on the wing's local domain controller. Testing finds wing users and computers but never the Medical printer. Which assessment explains the result and the fix?

answers.text: Move the tool to the Medical site, since search results follow physical subnet placement.
answers.rationale: Sites map the physical network by subnet, so moving the tool changes its placement, not the directory data it searches.

answers.text: Search the schema partition, since it defines classes for objects in each domain.
answers.rationale: The schema holds class and attribute definitions, not the printer object that the tool must locate.

answers.text: Search a global catalog server, since a domain partition holds objects for one domain.
answers.rationale: A domain partition stores one domain's objects, while a global catalog includes objects from all domains in the forest.

answers.text: Search the configuration partition, since it stores user and printer objects forest-wide.
answers.rationale: The configuration partition stores configuration objects for the forest, not users or printers.

questions.stem: A new server joins the domain to host the squadron's training database. It does not authenticate logons, enforce domain policy or take part in directory replication. An airman records it as a domain client because it has a computer account in Active Directory (AD). Which classification fits best?

answers.text: A domain controller, since it joined the domain and now holds a computer account.
answers.rationale: Domain controllers authenticate users, enforce policies and handle replication, which this server does not do.

answers.text: A domain client, since a computer account is the defining trait it shows.
answers.rationale: A domain client runs a user's desktop environment; this server provides a database to others for a dedicated purpose.

answers.text: A global catalog server, since users in several domains query its training database.
answers.rationale: A global catalog includes directory objects from all domains in a forest, not an application's database.

answers.text: A member server, since it belongs to the domain but performs no controller duties.
answers.rationale: A member server belongs to a domain but is not the domain controller, matching the duties described.

questions.stem: A design draft creates a Finance Organizational Unit (OU) holding user accounts, then nests three new user accounts beneath MSgt Rush's existing user object so that MSgt Rush's team appears grouped. The import tool rejects the three nested accounts. MSgt Rush still wants the team shown as one group within Finance. Which change resolves the error and meets that request?

keywords.text: beneath MSgt Rush's existing user object

answers.text: Create a team Organizational Unit (OU) inside Finance and move the accounts there.
answers.rationale: An Organizational Unit (OU) can hold users and other OUs, while each user object is a leaf that cannot contain other objects.

answers.text: Store the three accounts as attributes on MSgt Rush's existing user object instead.
answers.rationale: Attributes describe an object, such as a name or phone number; they do not hold other directory objects.

answers.text: Delegate control to MSgt Rush's account so it is allowed to hold the nested accounts.
answers.rationale: Delegated permissions change who manages objects; they do not let a leaf object contain other objects.

answers.text: Place the team in a new site by subnet range rather than a Finance Organizational Unit (OU).
answers.rationale: Sites map the physical network by subnet and do not provide the logical grouping inside Finance.

questions.stem: An audit of the Finance Organizational Unit (OU) finds that each user object's attributes are accurate, yet members of the Supply group can edit those accounts. No one has changed the class definitions, and the accounts sit in the correct organizational unit. MSgt Rush must name the first item to examine to correct the defect. Which item fits?

keywords.text: members of the Supply group can edit those accounts

answers.text: Schema definitions for user objects, to remove the editable attributes.
answers.rationale: Class definitions are unchanged and describe object structure, not which groups may edit an object.

answers.text: The position of the Organizational Unit (OU) in the domain tree, to move the accounts to another OU.
answers.rationale: The accounts are already in the correct Organizational Unit (OU), so moving them does not address who can edit them.

answers.text: The Access Control List (ACL) entries on the accounts, to remove Supply's edit permissions.
The user objects' attribute values, to reset the fields that Supply has edited.
answers.rationale: The attributes are accurate; the defect is which group is allowed to change the accounts.

questions.stem: A project wants to retire a site's domain controller and replace it with an appliance that can locate objects from all domains in the forest. Users at the site will still sign in to the domain through that box each morning. MSgt Rush must decide what to confirm before approving the swap. Which question should the review answer?

keywords.text: sign in to the domain through that box

answers.text: Whether the appliance uses the same object class definitions as the current controller.
answers.rationale: Shared definitions say nothing about whether the appliance can carry out the controller's duties.

answers.text: Whether the appliance returns objects from other domains when users search the forest.
answers.rationale: Forest-wide search is already stated; it does not show that users can sign in through the appliance.

answers.text: Whether the appliance can be installed in the same site and subnet range.
answers.rationale: Physical placement does not show that the appliance performs the directory services users need.

answers.text: Whether the appliance can replace the controller's user authentication, policies and replication.
answers.rationale: Domain controllers are responsible for authenticating users, enforcing policies and replication, beyond searching the directory.

questions.stem: After a weekend change to delegation on the Supply Organizational Unit (OU), the Supply help desk reports that it cannot reset Supply passwords. No hardware alarms appeared, and nobody has retried a reset since the report. MSgt Rush proposes restoring the domain controller from backup. Which response best fits the troubleshooting guidance?

keywords.text: nobody has retried a reset since the report

answers.text: Reproduce the failed reset, then review the weekend delegation change.
answers.rationale: Duplicating the problem is the first troubleshooting step, and most Active Directory (AD) problems are administrative errors, so the weekend delegation change is the likeliest cause to review next.

answers.text: Restore the domain controller from backup, since a server fault is likelier.
answers.rationale: No hardware alarm appeared, and most Active Directory (AD) problems are administrative errors, not server faults.

answers.text: Review the weekend delegation change, then reproduce the reset if it looks correct.
answers.rationale: Reviewing the change before anyone retries the reset reverses the troubleshooting order.

answers.text: Rebuild the Supply Organizational Unit (OU), since structure faults cause most problems.
answers.rationale: Most Active Directory (AD) problems are administrative errors, not structure faults.

questions.stem: An asset team adds 40 network printers to the directory and wants staff to search for them by building and floor. One proposal creates an Organizational Unit (OU) per floor and treats printers as data on it; another stores building and floor with each printer. The team asks how the directory represents this information. Which interpretation fits?

keywords.text: stores building and floor with each printer

answers.text: Each floor is an Organizational Unit (OU), and its printers are attributes of that unit.
answers.rationale: A printer is a single entity, and attributes describe an entity rather than standing in for other entities.

answers.text: Each printer is an object, and its building and floor are attribute values.
answers.rationale: An object represents a single entity, and attributes such as location define and describe it.

answers.text: Each printer is a schema class, and its building and floor are separate objects.
answers.rationale: The schema defines classes and attributes; one printer is an instance, and its location describes it.

answers.text: Each building is a site, and each printer is an attribute of that site.
answers.rationale: Sites map the physical network by subnet, and a printer is an entity rather than a descriptive value.

questions.stem: A workstation can open the intranet portal at 10.10.10.1 but fails when users enter rhope-ops.github.io/icf. An airman runs a reverse lookup of 10.10.10.1, and it correctly returns rhope-ops.github.io. MSgt Rush asks what that test proves and what to test next. Which assessment is best?

answers.text: The reverse result leaves name-to-address resolution untested, so run a forward lookup.
answers.rationale: A forward lookup resolves a hostname to an Internet Protocol (IP) address, which is the direction that is failing.

answers.text: The reverse result proves forward resolution works, so the fault lies in the portal server.
answers.rationale: Address-to-name success does not show that the hostname resolves to an address.

answers.text: The reverse result shows a zone transfer failed, so force the secondary to synchronize.
answers.rationale: Nothing in the symptoms compares two servers' zone copies, and the reverse answer was correct.

answers.text: Repeat the reverse lookup from a second client to confirm the address-to-name mapping.
answers.rationale: This retests the direction that already works and still leaves the failing name lookup untested.

questions.stem: A firewall log shows repeated connections from 10.10.10.1 but records no hostname. MSgt Rush runs a reverse lookup on 10.10.10.1 against the unit's Domain Name System (DNS) server and gets no name back, although users reach every server by name. The server's one zone was created for forward lookups. An airman suggests restarting the server. Which action best explains and fixes the empty result?

keywords.text: one zone was created for forward lookups

answers.text: Run forward lookups on guessed hostnames until one returns 10.10.10.1, since a reverse lookup needs a name first.
answers.rationale: A reverse lookup starts from an address, which MSgt Rush already holds, and guessing hostnames leaves the empty reverse result unexplained.

answers.text: Create a reverse lookup zone, since the server's only zone holds records for forward lookups, not reverse ones.
answers.rationale: A zone is designated for forward or reverse lookups when it is created, so a server whose one zone is for forward lookups returns no name for an address.

answers.text: Add an alias record for 10.10.10.1, since an alias record maps a logged address back to its host.
answers.rationale: An alias record creates another name for a host name; it does not map an address back to a name.

answers.text: Restart the server, since name lookups that work show a reverse lookup zone is already in place.
answers.rationale: Domain Name System (DNS) operation does not require a zone for address lookups, so working name lookups prove nothing, and a restart adds no records.

questions.stem: The wing replaces its mail forwarder with a new Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) host, but the domain's authoritative Domain Name System (DNS) servers stay the same. An airman proposes editing the name server records so mail reaches the new host. MSgt Rush notes the zone's administrative details list a contact email. Which correction to the plan is best?

keywords.text: authoritative Domain Name System (DNS) servers stay the same

answers.text: Update the Start of Authority (SOA) record, since it holds the domain's email settings.
answers.rationale: Start of Authority (SOA) holds administrative details such as contact email, serial number and zone sync, not the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) host.

answers.text: Update the Host Information (HINFO) records to describe the new mail host's Operating System (OS).
answers.rationale: Host Information (HINFO) describes a host's Operating System (OS) and Central Processing Unit (CPU) type, not where the domain's mail goes.

answers.text: Add a Canonical Name (CNAME) record so the old forwarder's name becomes an alias of the new host.
answers.rationale: An alias gives a host another name; the record that indicates the domain's Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) host is a different type.

answers.text: Update the Mail Exchanger (MX) record and leave the name server records unchanged.
answers.rationale: A Mail Exchanger (MX) record indicates the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) host, and name server records change only when authoritative servers change.

questions.stem: Domain-joined workstations at a new site must find a domain controller to log on, but they are not configured with any controller's hostname. The controllers are running, and the zone already maps their hostnames to addresses. Which record type best fills the gap?

keywords.text: not configured with any controller's hostname

answers.text: A Service (SRV) record that locates a host providing a specific network service.
answers.rationale: A service record locates a host that can provide a specific network service, such as a domain controller.

answers.text: A Host Information (HINFO) record that lists each controller's Operating System (OS) and Central Processing Unit (CPU).
answers.rationale: Host Information (HINFO) describes a known host's Operating System (OS) and Central Processing Unit (CPU) type; it does not find the host.

answers.text: A Canonical Name (CNAME) record that gives each controller a shorter alias.
answers.rationale: An alias still requires the client to know a name, and these clients know no controller name.

answers.text: A Start of Authority (SOA) record that lists the zone's administrative details.
answers.rationale: Start of Authority (SOA) holds administrative details for the zone, not a way to find a host by its service.

questions.stem: A squadron needs two authoritative Domain Name System (DNS) servers for its zone. Administrators will edit records on the first server, the second server has to answer queries for the zone if the first fails, and no one should be able to edit records on the second server. Which design meets all three conditions?

keywords.text: no one should be able to edit records on the second server

answers.text: Run two primary servers and have administrators enter each change on both of them.
answers.rationale: Two editable master copies break the condition that the second server cannot be edited.

answers.text: Edit a primary's master zone and copy it to a secondary by zone transfer.
answers.rationale: A primary holds the master copy, and a secondary obtains read-only zone copies by zone transfer yet stays authoritative.

answers.text: Make the first server primary and the second a caching-only name server.
answers.rationale: A caching-only server is not authoritative for any zone, so it cannot answer for the zone as required.

answers.text: Make the first server a secondary and the second a primary for the zone.
answers.rationale: This reverses the roles: edits belong on the master copy, and the read-only copy sits on the secondary.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush adds a record for a new file server on the primary Domain Name System (DNS) server at 0900. At 1000, clients that query the primary resolve the new name, while clients that query the secondary still get no answer for it. The secondary holds a read-only copy of the zone. Which item should MSgt Rush check?

keywords.text: clients that query the primary resolve the new name

answers.text: Whether the record was also typed directly into the secondary's zone file.
answers.rationale: The secondary's zone copy is read only and is obtained from the primary, not edited by hand.

answers.text: Whether the clients' cached answers have expired under their Time to Live (TTL).
answers.rationale: Clients of the primary already resolve the name, so the gap lies between the two servers' copies.

answers.text: Whether a zone transfer has brought the new record over to the secondary.
answers.rationale: A secondary obtains its zone files from the primary by zone transfer, which keeps the copies synchronized.

answers.text: Whether the secondary should be rebuilt as a server that caches lookups.
answers.rationale: A caching-only server is not authoritative for any zone, so it would not fix missing zone data.

questions.stem: A server at a remote site answers repeat lookups quickly from stored results, and those results expire when their Time to Live (TTL) ends. It holds no zone file and has never received a zone transfer. A proposal lists it as the site's secondary name server. Which classification is better supported?

keywords.text: has never received a zone transfer

answers.text: Primary, since it answers the site's queries from data it holds itself.
answers.rationale: A primary contains the master copy of a zone file, and this server holds no zone file.

answers.text: Secondary, since its repeated answers act as a read-only copy of the zone.
answers.rationale: A secondary obtains its zone files from a primary, and this server has never received a zone transfer.

answers.text: Non-recursive server, since it knows answers already and needs no further queries.
answers.rationale: Non-recursive describes a query answered without more rounds, not a type of name server.

answers.text: Caching-only, since stored lookup results do not make a server authoritative.
answers.rationale: A caching-only server caches results until the Time to Live (TTL) expires and is not authoritative for any zone.

questions.stem: A local name server resolved icf.rhope-ops.github.io 20 minutes ago and cached the answer, whose Time to Live (TTL) is 60 minutes. A second client now asks for the same name. MSgt Rush wonders whether another search from the root is needed now and whether the stored answer can be reused next week. Which assessment is correct?

answers.text: Answer from the cache now, and query again once the cached entry expires.
answers.rationale: Cached entries let the server answer other queries quickly, and they remain only until the Time to Live (TTL) expires.

answers.text: Answer from the cache now and keep reusing it, since a past success stays valid.
answers.rationale: Cached entries are kept for a limited time set by the Time to Live (TTL), so next week the answer will have expired.

answers.text: Query the root server again, since a cached answer serves the first client alone.
answers.rationale: Caching lets the local server respond more quickly to other queries, including this second client.

answers.text: Request a zone transfer for github.io before reusing the cached answer.
answers.rationale: Zone transfer synchronizes servers holding a zone; a local cache answers lookups without one.

questions.stem: A client asks its local Domain Name System (DNS) server for icf.rhope-ops.github.io. The local server does not know the address, so it sends the request on to the root server, which sends it to the .io server, which sends it to the authoritative server for github.io. The reply then passes back through each server to the client. Which query type does this exchange show?

answers.text: A reverse lookup, since the answer travels back through the servers in reverse order.
answers.rationale: A reverse lookup resolves an address to a name, but the client supplied a hostname.

answers.text: A recursive query, since each server carries the lookup onward until it is answered.
answers.rationale: In a recursive query the resolver must return an answer or an error, and here each server carried the request onward.

answers.text: An iterative query, since the local server queries each level and collects the replies.
answers.rationale: Here the root and .io servers passed the request on instead of returning information to the local server.

answers.text: A non-recursive query, since the client receives one answer without asking again.
answers.rationale: A non-recursive query is answered from known data without additional rounds, but this exchange needed several.

questions.stem: A client asks its local Domain Name System (DNS) server for icf.rhope-ops.github.io. The local server queries the root, which replies with information about the .io server. The local server then asks the .io server, which replies with information about the authoritative server for github.io. Finally the local server asks that server and receives the address. Which query type does this exchange show?

keywords.text: replies with information about the .io server

answers.text: A zone transfer, since each server sends zone information back to the local server.
answers.rationale: Zone transfer synchronizes zone copies between servers; these replies answer one lookup.

answers.text: A reverse lookup, since each reply flows back toward the local server.
answers.rationale: A reverse lookup resolves an address to a name, but the client asked about a hostname.

answers.text: An iterative query, since each contacted server returns the best information it has.
answers.rationale: The resolver provides the best answer it can, and the root returned .io server information to the local server.

answers.text: A recursive query, since each contacted server resolves the full name before replying.
answers.rationale: The root and .io servers did not resolve the name; they returned information about the next server.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush documents the Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) icf.rhope-ops.github.io for a lab server. The documentation template lists each label with its level in the Domain Name System (DNS) hierarchy. An airman enters rhope-ops as the top-level domain because it sits next to the host label. Which breakdown should replace the entry?

keywords.text: it sits next to the host label

answers.text: io is the host, github a subdomain, rhope-ops second level, and icf top level.
answers.rationale: This reverses the hierarchy, which starts at the right with the top-level domain.

answers.text: rhope-ops is the top level, github second level, io a subdomain, and icf the host.
answers.rationale: The top-level domain is the rightmost label, so io, not rhope-ops, holds that level.

answers.text: icf is the host, rhope-ops second level, github a subdomain, and io top level.
answers.rationale: Moving left from io, the next label is second level, so github and rhope-ops are swapped here.

answers.text: icf is the host, rhope-ops a subdomain, github second level, and io top level.
answers.rationale: Reading from the right, the levels run top level, then second level, then subdomain (third level), then host.

questions.stem: An airman's resilience-exercise memo states that the root layer of the Domain Name System (DNS) is 13 physical machines, because the root zone lists 13 server addresses, so losing 13 machines would end root service worldwide. MSgt Rush agrees the root zone holds 13 server addresses but asks which conclusion the memo should reach instead. Which critique is best supported?

keywords.text: the root zone lists 13 server addresses

answers.text: Thirteen limits addresses, not hardware; each address has a server cluster, so lookups continue.
answers.rationale: The architecture caps the root zone at 13 addresses, each address has clusters of servers, and over 600 physical root servers existed at last count.

answers.text: The memo is right, since the architecture caps the root zone at 13 servers, one machine each.
answers.rationale: The architecture caps addresses at 13, but each address has clusters of servers, so the machine count is far higher.

answers.text: Thirteen counts the top-level domain servers, so the root layer sits above a larger group.
answers.rationale: The 13 figure is the maximum number of server addresses in the root zone, not a count of top-level domain servers.

answers.text: Thirteen is outdated; the root zone now lists over 600 server addresses, so 13 losses barely matter.
answers.rationale: Over 600 was the physical server count at last count; the root zone still has a maximum of 13 server addresses.

questions.stem: A zone audit asks for three items in order: the record that holds the zone's serial number and contact address, the records a resolver uses to find the servers that answer for the domain, and the process that keeps the secondary's read-only copy current. Which answer lists them in order?

answers.text: Mail Exchanger (MX), Host Information (HINFO), and reverse lookup, respectively.
answers.rationale: Mail Exchanger (MX) indicates a mail host; the contact email in the first item is zone administrative data.

answers.text: Service (SRV), Canonical Name (CNAME), and forward lookup, respectively.
answers.rationale: A service record locates service hosts, an alias renames a host, and a forward lookup resolves one name.

answers.text: Start of Authority (SOA), Name Server, and zone transfer, respectively.
answers.rationale: Start of Authority (SOA) holds zone administrative details, name server records identify servers to contact, and zone transfer copies zones.

answers.text: Name Server, zone transfer, and Start of Authority (SOA), respectively.
answers.rationale: This puts a record in the process slot and the process in a record slot.

questions.stem: After a Domain Name System (DNS) server rebuild, a site's domain controller is running and responds when reached by its Internet Protocol (IP) address, yet workstations that rely on DNS to find a domain controller fail to log on. The rebuilt zone was restored from an old copy. Which conclusion best fits the evidence?

answers.text: The controller's directory service has likely failed, so restart it before checking Domain Name System (DNS).
answers.rationale: The controller is running and reachable; the failure appears only when clients rely on Domain Name System (DNS) to find it.

answers.text: The workstations' computer accounts are probably corrupt, so rejoin them to the domain.
answers.rationale: The failure began with the Domain Name System (DNS) rebuild and affects workstations that depend on DNS to find the controller.

answers.text: The schema was likely damaged by the rebuild, so restore the class definitions first.
answers.rationale: The rebuild changed the Domain Name System (DNS) server, not the directory's class definitions.

answers.text: The restored zone likely lacks the records that let clients locate the controller, so re-register them.
answers.rationale: Locating a domain controller depends on registration of information in Domain Name System (DNS) and the availability of that information.

questions.stem: A base runs two Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) servers on one network for resilience. Both use the same address range, and an offer delay on the second server lets the first normally answer first. After the first server reboots, two clients report the same address. Which review finding best explains the conflict and the fix?

keywords.text: Both use the same address range

answers.text: Give each server a unique range; the delay changes timing, not which addresses each server leases.
answers.rationale: Scopes on multiple Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) servers must be unique to avoid leasing duplicate addresses; a delay only postpones the offer.

answers.text: Lengthen the delay so the second server has time to learn the first server's leases.
answers.rationale: A delay is how long a server waits before sending its offer; waiting longer shares no lease information.

answers.text: Shorten the lease duration so duplicate addresses return to the pool before clients collide.
answers.rationale: Lease duration sets how long an address is loaned; it does not stop two servers leasing the same range.

answers.text: Keep the shared range but give the two scopes different names so each server tracks its own leases.
answers.rationale: A scope name is a label; it does not stop two servers from leasing the same addresses.

questions.stem: A network printer has a hand-set address, 192.168.1.40, inside a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) scope of 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.254, and last week a laptop was leased that same address. A file server on the subnet leases its address from the scope but must keep 192.168.1.50 every time it renews. Which scope plan best meets both needs?

keywords.text: must keep 192.168.1.50 every time it renews

answers.text: Exclude both 192.168.1.40 and 192.168.1.50 from the scope, leaving the rest of the range leasable.
answers.rationale: Excluded addresses are not distributed by the server, so the file server, a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) client, would not receive 192.168.1.50.

answers.text: Exclude 192.168.1.40 from the scope, and create a reservation of 192.168.1.50 for the file server.
answers.rationale: Excluding the hand-set address stops Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) leasing it, and a reservation makes the file server lease the same address each time.

answers.text: Reserve 192.168.1.40 for the printer, and exclude 192.168.1.50 for the file server.
answers.rationale: This swaps the tools: the excluded address is not distributed, so the file server, which leases from Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), would lose 192.168.1.50.

answers.text: Shorten the lease so 192.168.1.40 returns sooner, and create a reservation of 192.168.1.50.
answers.rationale: A shorter loan still leaves 192.168.1.40 leasable, so another client can receive the printer's address again.

questions.stem: An airman's change request for a new Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) scope lists the name 'Ops Floor 2', the description 'Second-floor workstations', exclusions for 10.1.2.5 and 10.1.2.6 used by printers, and an eight-day lease. MSgt Rush rejects the request before setup begins. Which gap best justifies the rejection?

answers.text: The lease is too long, so the scope should be shortened before it is created.
answers.rationale: Lease duration is how long an address is loaned; it does not define which addresses the scope holds.

answers.text: The exclusions should be removed, since excluded addresses do not belong in a new scope.
answers.rationale: Administrators set aside static addresses within a scope by excluding them, so exclusions belong in a scope.

answers.text: It gives no start address, end address or subnet mask, so the exclusions have no range.
answers.rationale: Scope setup needs starting and ending addresses and a subnet mask; a name, description and lease do not supply them.

answers.text: It lacks an offer delay, which is the setting that decides which addresses are offered.
answers.rationale: A delay only sets how long the server waits before sending an offer, not which addresses are offered.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush runs a main and a backup Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server on one network. Two goals are set: clients should keep an address for one day before it must be renewed, and the backup server should wait two seconds before proposing addresses so the main server answers first. Which configuration meets both goals?

keywords.text: wait two seconds before proposing addresses

answers.text: Set the one day as offer delay and the two seconds as lease duration on the main server.
answers.rationale: This reverses the settings: the lease is the loan period and the delay is the wait before an offer.

answers.text: Set a one-day lease duration and add a two-second offer delay on the main server.
