answers.rationale: Reported problems are fixed in maintenance, and in testing developers input random invalid data to check for crashes, a process known as fuzzing.

answers.text: Fix the crashes in deployment and run fuzzing in implementation, since the code is written and installed there
answers.rationale: Deployment installs the application on the production servers and implementation is where the code gets written; reports and fuzzing belong to other phases, not these.

answers.text: Fix the crashes in implementation and skip fuzzing, since written code needs no further checks
answers.rationale: The code must be checked in testing for crashes and other bugs, so written code does need further checks.

questions.stem: An airman signs in to a website from a shared wireless network. The website stores logon information in cookies, and MSgt Rush suspects that someone is tapping into the traffic. MSgt Rush proposes stricter file permissions on the web server. Which response is best supported?

keywords.text: someone is tapping into the traffic

answers.text: Tighten the file permissions on the server, since permissions keep tapped data unreadable while it is in transit
answers.rationale: File permissions do not protect the file contents from being read while the files are in transit.

answers.text: Encrypt the files stored on the web server, since storage encryption stops anyone tapping the link
answers.rationale: Encrypting stored files protects data at rest; it does not stop someone who taps into the communication.

answers.text: Encrypt the communication channel, since a tapper could otherwise read the logon information carried in cookies
answers.rationale: Encrypting information in transit means someone who taps into the communication cannot read it, including cookie contents such as logon information.

answers.text: Delete the cookies after each visit, since that makes the tapped traffic unreadable to the person tapping
answers.rationale: Removing cookies later does not make the traffic unreadable while it travels across the network.

questions.stem: A bank website's code references another web page that takes a user's unexpired cookies for authentication. An airman asks how to reduce the risk. MSgt Rush suggests patching the web server alone. Which plan is best supported?

answers.text: Patch the web server alone, since patches close the cookie weakness without other changes to the website or the browser
answers.rationale: Patches remove vulnerabilities in software, but this weakness comes from unexpired cookies that users and developers must manage.

answers.text: Have users refuse to run ActiveX controls, since the referenced page runs code that takes the cookies
answers.rationale: Refusing to run ActiveX controls is a sound browser practice, but it does not stop another page from reusing the user's cookies.

answers.text: Apply input validation to the logon form, since it blocks pages that reference other pages from using cookies
answers.rationale: Input validation ensures entered data and button presses give the desired result; it does not remove unexpired cookies.

answers.text: Have users deny Remember Me and developers set cookies to expire quickly, since the attack relies on unexpired cookies
answers.rationale: Remember Me should be denied by users in the browser and developers should set cookies to expire quickly to avoid cross-site request forgery.

questions.stem: A laptop holding mission files is stolen, and the thief bypasses its file permissions. MSgt Rush proposes encrypting the communications channel that the laptop uses when it synchronizes the files with a server. Which assessment is best supported?

keywords.text: synchronizes the files with a server

answers.text: The proposal is enough, since channel encryption also keeps the stored files unreadable on the laptop
answers.rationale: Encrypting the communications channel protects information in transit; it does not make stored files unreadable.

answers.text: The proposal does not help, since encrypting the files in storage keeps them unreadable after permissions are bypassed
answers.rationale: Permissions can be bypassed with physical access, and encrypting the file in storage keeps the data unreadable, while channel encryption covers only data traveling between systems.

answers.text: Stricter file permissions would fix it, since a thief with physical access is stopped by those permissions
answers.rationale: Hackers with physical access can normally bypass the permissions set by the system, so stricter permissions do not fix it.

answers.text: Logging each file access with accounting would fix it, since a record of the thief's access keeps the stored files protected
answers.rationale: Accounting logs user activity and tracks usage; it does not make the stored files unreadable.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush wants one deployment that watches traffic across many systems on the base network and automatically takes corrective action against suspicious activity, not merely logging it. An airman proposes a Host-Based Intrusion Detection System (HIDS) on the main server. Which deployment is best supported?

answers.text: A Host-Based Intrusion Detection System (HIDS), since it detects, logs and alerts on activity at one host
answers.rationale: A Host-Based Intrusion Detection System (HIDS) logs and alerts rather than acting, and it watches a single host.

answers.text: A Network-Based Intrusion Detection System (NIDS), since it watches many systems and alerts administrators about suspicious activity
answers.rationale: A Network-Based Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) monitors multiple systems but only logs and alerts; it takes no corrective action.

answers.text: A Host-Based Intrusion Prevention System (HIPS), since it actively protects a host by stopping attacks
answers.rationale: A Host-Based Intrusion Prevention System (HIPS) stops attacks on its host, but it does not watch activity across multiple systems.

answers.text: A network-based Intrusion Prevention System (IPS), since it watches many systems and takes corrective action
answers.rationale: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) and Intrusion Prevention Systems (IPSs) can be network-based, which monitors multiple systems, and an IPS takes corrective action.

questions.stem: A base installs a Network-Based Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) across three network segments. Sensors sit on segments A and C, and the analysis engine and console work normally, yet nothing from segment B ever appears in the alerts. MSgt Rush suggests adding a second console. Which fix is best supported?

keywords.text: nothing from segment B ever appears in the alerts

answers.text: Add a second console, since alerts and notifications are sent there and MSgt Rush could review them
answers.rationale: A console receives alerts and is used to configure the system; it does not collect traffic from a segment.

answers.text: Place a sensor on segment B, since a sensor on each segment collects its traffic and forwards it for analysis
answers.rationale: A sensor placed on each network segment collects the segment's traffic and forwards it to the analysis engine or a collector.

answers.text: Reconfigure the analysis engine to collect segment B's traffic itself, since it already examines the packets it receives
answers.rationale: The analysis engine analyzes packets it receives from a sensor or collector; it does not collect traffic from a segment.

answers.text: Add a collector on segment B, since collectors gather traffic from segments directly for the engine
answers.rationale: A collector gathers traffic from the sensors, not from the segments, so segment B would still lack a sensor.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush has disabled booting from everything but the primary storage drive on a workstation, so an attacker cannot start another Operating System (OS) from a disc. An airman points out that the attacker could still open the setup program and re-enable booting from the optical drive. Which additional step keeps the attacker from changing the setup program?

answers.text: Install a Hardware Security Module (HSM), since it holds cryptographic processors on a separate card in the workstation
answers.rationale: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) stores cryptographic processors on an add-on card; it does not stop someone from changing the boot settings.

answers.text: Enable Full Disk Encryption (FDE), since it protects the drive in case of theft or loss
answers.rationale: Full Disk Encryption (FDE) protects the drive contents if the system is stolen or lost, but the setup program stays open to change.

answers.text: Enable a bootup password, since it protects the setup program that decides which device the system boots from
answers.rationale: A bootup password protects the setup program itself, which determines what storage device to boot from, and it is required before getting to the Operating System (OS).

answers.text: Enable Secure Boot, since it checks that the bootup files are digitally signed before they run
answers.rationale: Secure boot runs only signed bootup files, but it does not stop someone from changing the setup program.

questions.stem: An airman's laptop holding mission data is lost on a flight. MSgt Rush wants the entire hard disk drive protected, not only selected files, and wants the cryptographic keys kept in a hardware component instead of on the drive. Which design is best supported?

answers.text: Full Disk Encryption (FDE) with a Trusted Platform Module (TPM), since it covers the drive and holds the keys
answers.rationale: Full Disk Encryption (FDE) encrypts an entire drive in case of loss, and a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) stores the cryptographic keys used for it.

answers.text: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) in place of drive encryption, since it is an add-on device with processors
answers.rationale: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) holds cryptographic processors on a separate card; it is not the encryption of an entire drive.

answers.text: A bootup password with Secure Boot, since the password guards the setup program and the bootup files are signed
answers.rationale: A bootup password protects the setup program and Secure Boot checks signed bootup files; neither encrypts the drive or stores keys.

answers.text: Secure Boot, since it signs the bootup files and also keeps the cryptographic keys for the laptop
answers.rationale: Secure boot has the system digitally sign bootup files; it does not encrypt the drive or store the keys.

questions.stem: A base rolls out Single Sign-On (SSO) so airmen log on once to reach many servers, using a username and a password. MSgt Rush worries that one stolen password would expose all of those servers, wants to keep the single logon, and proposes adding a second password prompt. Which improvement is best supported?

keywords.text: one stolen password would expose all of those servers

answers.text: Add a second password prompt, since two prompts make the logon multifactor
answers.rationale: A second password is still something the user knows, and combining items from the same factor category is not multifactor authentication.

answers.text: Add a token the airman has, since a different factor category makes the logon multifactor
answers.rationale: A token is something you have, and multifactor authentication combines factors such as a token and a password, which limits the damage of one stolen password.

answers.text: Add a Personal Identification Number (PIN), since a PIN is a separate factor from a password
answers.rationale: Passwords and Personal Identification Numbers (PINs) are both examples of something you know, so they are one factor category, not two.

answers.text: Add a longer username, since username length counts as a second factor
answers.rationale: A username plus a password is still based on two kinds of something you know, not a second factor, however long the username is.

questions.stem: A mission portal grants access only when three checks pass: the airman's password, a login from an Internet Protocol (IP) address on the base network, and a typing pattern that matches the stored sample. MSgt Rush calls this three-factor authentication. Which statement is best supported?

keywords.text: a typing pattern that matches the stored sample

answers.text: It is two-factor, since the location and the typing pattern are both something you are
answers.rationale: A location is somewhere you are and a typing pattern is something you do, so they are different categories.

answers.text: It is two-factor, since the password and the typing pattern are both something you know
answers.rationale: A typing pattern is based on user habits, which is something you do, not something you know.

answers.text: It is three-factor, since the password, location and typing pattern are in three different categories
answers.rationale: Passwords are something you know, location by Internet Protocol (IP) address is somewhere you are, and typing patterns are something you do.

answers.text: It is single-factor, since the three checks happen together during one logon at the portal
answers.rationale: Factors are counted by category, not by how many checks happen in one logon.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush's team is deploying a web application with its default options. MSgt Rush wants strong security and plans to turn off every optional setting, even though the mission depends on one function of the application. An airman recommends standard hardening. Which plan is best supported?

answers.text: Turn off every optional setting, since the strongest security comes before any mission function
answers.rationale: Options should be modified for security only if the necessary functionality is not impeded, and the mission depends on one function.

answers.text: Disable the features nobody needs and set security options, since configuration must not impede needed functionality
answers.rationale: Features that are not necessary should be disabled, and options that make the application more secure should be set if the necessary functionality is not impeded.

answers.text: Keep the default options, since hardening cannot protect an application that must stay available for the mission to continue
answers.rationale: Application hardening applies to applications and prevents issues in the first place, but default options leave unneeded features enabled.

answers.text: Disable the features the mission needs, since hardening removes the functions that users depend on
answers.rationale: Hardening disables features that are not necessary, not the ones that the mission needs.

questions.stem: An airman finds that packets reached a server through the network's packet-filtering firewall although no connection had been set up through a three-way handshake; an attacker had altered their headers to show an allowed address and port. MSgt Rush proposes adding more address and port rules. Which firewall choice and reason best close the gap?

keywords.text: no connection had been set up through a three-way handshake

answers.text: Keep packet filtering, since it checks whether each packet fits an established conversation.
answers.rationale: A packet-filtering firewall decides from the header's addresses and ports, which the attacker altered; it does not check the conversation.

answers.text: Switch to stateful packet inspection, since it checks whether each packet fits an established conversation.
answers.rationale: Stateful packet inspection looks at the context of the conversation, so a packet that arrives without an established three-way handshake is not allowed inside.

answers.text: Keep packet filtering with more address and port rules, since it reads each packet header.
answers.rationale: More rules still read only the header, and the attacker altered the headers to show an allowed address and port, so the packets would still pass.

answers.text: Switch to stateful packet inspection, since it reads more address and port fields in each header.
answers.rationale: The attacker altered the header fields, so reading more of them would not reveal the missing handshake; the reason given does not fit the gap.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush must place a proxy in front of the unit's workstations. The airman reports that no software may be installed on the workstations and that their applications cannot be reconfigured. Which proxy type and method of directing clients to it meets both constraints?

keywords.text: no software may be installed on the workstations

answers.text: A nontransparent proxy, with a proxy client installed and the applications pointed at the proxy server
answers.rationale: A nontransparent proxy requires a proxy client, or agent, and configured applications, which the reported constraints do not allow.

answers.text: A transparent proxy, with a proxy client installed on each workstation
answers.rationale: A transparent proxy does not require a client, so installing one breaks the no-software constraint.

answers.text: A transparent proxy, with the default gateway setting pointed at the proxy server
answers.rationale: A transparent proxy needs no software or configuration on the client; the default gateway setting simply points to the proxy server, which meets both constraints.

answers.text: A nontransparent proxy, with the default gateway setting pointed at the proxy server
answers.rationale: A nontransparent proxy still needs a proxy client and configured applications, which the reported constraints do not allow, whatever the default gateway setting.

questions.stem: The unit's public web server and mail server sit on its internal network. MSgt Rush must let outside systems send requests to them after each request is checked, and the airmen's own Internet browsing must be handled the other way round. Which proxy arrangement fits?

answers.text: A reverse proxy for the outside requests and a forward proxy for the airmen's browsing
answers.rationale: A reverse proxy forwards requests from the Internet to internal servers after checking them, and a forward proxy retrieves Internet resources for internal clients.

answers.text: A forward proxy for the outside requests and a reverse proxy for the airmen's browsing
answers.rationale: The directions are swapped: a forward proxy retrieves resources for clients, but it is a reverse proxy that admits requests from the Internet.

answers.text: A reverse proxy for both the outside requests and the airmen's browsing
answers.rationale: A reverse proxy serves requests from the Internet to internal servers; it does not retrieve Internet resources for the airmen.

answers.text: A forward proxy for both the outside requests and the airmen's browsing
answers.rationale: A forward proxy retrieves resources for clients; it does not admit outside requests to the internal servers after checking them.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush wants an airman's desktop restrictions to stay in force on whichever workstation the airman logs on to, and also wants a password policy enforced on every workstation. How should the two requirements be assigned in a group policy?

keywords.text: whichever workstation the airman logs on to

answers.text: The desktop restrictions as computer settings and the password policy as user settings
answers.rationale: Desktop restrictions set as computer settings would stay with one workstation, and a password policy set as user settings would not be enforced on the system.

answers.text: Both the desktop restrictions and the password policy as user settings
answers.rationale: A password policy set as user settings would not be enforced on each workstation.

answers.text: Both the desktop restrictions and the password policy as computer settings
answers.rationale: Desktop restrictions set as computer settings would not follow the airman between workstations.

answers.text: The desktop restrictions as user settings and the password policy as computer settings
answers.rationale: User settings apply to a user on any machine and restrict desktops, while computer settings enforce password policies on a system.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush needs a Cisco router access list that permits one protocol from a single source address to one destination server. An airman proposes a standard access list because it is simpler to write. Which list should be used, and why?

keywords.text: one protocol from a single source address to one destination server

answers.text: A standard access list, since it controls traffic by source and destination addresses plus protocol information
answers.rationale: That describes the list numbered 100 and above; a standard access list uses only the source address.

answers.text: An extended access list, since it controls traffic by source and destination addresses plus protocol information
answers.rationale: An extended access list can control traffic by both source and destination addresses as well as protocol information, which the rule needs.

answers.text: A standard access list, since it permits or denies traffic by the source address alone
answers.rationale: A standard access list uses only the source address, so it cannot match the destination server or the protocol.

answers.text: An extended access list, since it permits or denies traffic by the source address alone
answers.rationale: Source-only filtering describes a standard access list; an extended list adds the destination and protocol information.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush is setting up the edge firewall for the unit's Internet-facing web server, which must keep serving its pages to the public. An airman proposes allowing all traffic and blocking ports as attacks appear. Which configuration should MSgt Rush use instead?

keywords.text: must keep serving its pages to the public

answers.text: Allow all traffic, then block ports as attacks appear
answers.rationale: Allowing everything by default leaves the web server exposed until each attack is blocked, which is not the default configuration.

answers.text: Block all traffic, then add exceptions for every port the server could use
answers.rationale: Exceptions are for the ports on which web server traffic runs, 443 and 80, not for every port the server could use.

answers.text: Block all traffic, then add exceptions only for ports 443 and 80
answers.rationale: Firewalls block all traffic by default, with exceptions for the ports on which web server traffic runs, 443 and 80.

answers.text: Allow all inbound traffic to the server, then block outbound traffic from it
answers.rationale: Letting every inbound packet through leaves the Internet-facing server open, which is not how a firewall default is set.

questions.stem: An airman takes a Windows laptop off the unit's network to work from other networks. The unit's edge firewall protects only traffic entering and leaving the unit's network. MSgt Rush wants the laptop protected wherever it connects. Which choice provides that protection?

answers.text: A hardware-based firewall at the edge of the unit's network
answers.rationale: A hardware-based firewall sits at the edge of the unit's network, which the laptop has left, so it no longer controls the laptop's traffic.

answers.text: A hardware-based firewall installed on the laptop
answers.rationale: A hardware-based firewall is a network-based device at the edge of a network, not something installed on a single system.

answers.text: A software-based firewall installed on the unit's edge router
answers.rationale: A software-based firewall protects the single system it is installed on, so one at the edge does not protect a laptop on other networks.

answers.text: A software-based firewall installed on the laptop
answers.rationale: A software-based firewall protects the single system it is installed on, so the laptop keeps its protection on any network.

questions.stem: Packets reaching the unit's web server belong to an established connection, so they pass the stateful checks. Some of those packets carry suspicious commands in their application data. MSgt Rush needs a control that can still deny them. Which control fits?

keywords.text: suspicious commands in their application data

answers.text: A stateful packet inspection firewall, since it checks the context of the conversation
answers.rationale: The packets already fit an established conversation, so context checking passes them; it does not inspect the payload for suspicious commands.

answers.text: An application-layer firewall, since it inspects the packet payload as well as the header
answers.rationale: An application-layer firewall combines packet-filtering and stateful features and, as an application/multi-purpose proxy, can inspect the payload and deny packets with suspicious commands.

answers.text: A packet-filtering firewall, since it filters on source and destination addresses and ports
answers.rationale: A packet-filtering firewall reads only header addresses and port numbers, which an attacker can alter, and not the payload.

answers.text: A standard access list on the router, since it permits or denies traffic by the source address
answers.rationale: A standard access list decides only by source address, so it cannot see suspicious commands inside application data.

questions.stem: A connection tries to establish itself on the unit's Linux system through its network card, and iptables finds no rule that matches it. MSgt Rush must name the table that controls traffic entering the system and say what iptables does with the unmatched connection. Which statement is correct?

keywords.text: iptables finds no rule that matches it

answers.text: The input table controls it, and iptables resorts to its default action
answers.rationale: The input table controls traffic into the Linux system, and when iptables finds no matching rule it resorts to the default action.

answers.text: The output table controls it, and iptables resorts to its default action
answers.rationale: The output table controls traffic leaving the Linux system, not traffic entering it.

answers.text: The input table controls it, and iptables forwards the connection on to another system
answers.rationale: Forwarding a packet on to another system is the forward table; iptables resorts to the default action when no rule matches.

answers.text: The forward table controls it, and iptables forwards the connection on to another system
answers.rationale: The forward table passes packets on to another system and does not control traffic entering the system through its network card.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush is documenting two controls. One is a set of New Technology File System (NTFS) permissions on a folder of a Windows server. The other is an access list on a Cisco router. Under which Access Control List (ACL) categories should the two controls be filed?

keywords.text: access list on a Cisco router

answers.text: The folder permissions as a networking Access Control List (ACL) and the router list as a file system ACL
answers.rationale: The categories are swapped: folder permissions on a Windows server are the file system category, but router access lists regulate network traffic.

answers.text: Both controls as file system Access Control Lists (ACLs)
answers.rationale: Only the folder permissions are a file system Access Control List (ACL); the router access list regulates inbound and outbound network traffic.

answers.text: Both controls as Active Directory (AD) Access Control Lists (ACLs)
answers.rationale: The Active Directory (AD) category covers the directory service that stores network resources, but neither of these controls is that service.

answers.text: The folder permissions as a file system Access Control List (ACL) and the router list as a networking ACL
answers.rationale: Securing a Windows folder with New Technology File System (NTFS) permissions is a file system Access Control List (ACL), and Cisco router access lists regulate traffic as networking ACLs.

questions.stem: A squadron's network places a Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between an external and an internal firewall, with the private Local Area Network (LAN) behind the internal firewall. An airman proposes opening a port on the internal firewall so Internet users can reach a file share on the private LAN. MSgt Rush must answer. Which response is best supported?

keywords.text: opening a port on the internal firewall

answers.text: Open the port on the internal firewall, since the external firewall already screens the Internet traffic.
answers.rationale: The internal firewall's purpose is to pass no traffic that originates from the Internet, so a port for Internet users defeats it whatever the external firewall screens.

answers.text: Move the share to a Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) server, since the internal firewall blocks Internet-originated traffic.
answers.rationale: The internal firewall passes no traffic that originates from the Internet, while the external firewall lets selected Internet traffic reach systems within the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

answers.text: Open a port on the external firewall alone, since the private Local Area Network (LAN) sits right behind it.
answers.rationale: The private Local Area Network (LAN) sits behind the internal firewall, so a port on the external firewall alone still leaves the internal firewall blocking the requests.

answers.text: Put a reverse proxy on the private Local Area Network (LAN), since it checks requests before passing them inward.
answers.rationale: A reverse proxy on the private Local Area Network (LAN) still needs Internet requests to cross the internal firewall, which passes no traffic that originates from the Internet.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush is placing two new systems in the squadron's firewall plan. The first is a network for visitors, who need only to check email and browse the web. The second is a web server that the public must reach. An airman asks which security zone suits each system. Which placement is best supported?

keywords.text: a web server that the public must reach

answers.text: Visitor network in the private zone; web server in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).
answers.rationale: Visitors typically do not need access to the private network, and the private zone is where the Local Area Network (LAN) resides behind a firewall that sends no traffic from other networks.

answers.text: Visitor network in the guest zone; web server in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).
answers.rationale: The guest zone gives visitors Internet access without access to any other security zone, and servers that the public must reach, such as a web server, belong in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

answers.text: Visitor network in the guest zone; web server in the public zone.
answers.rationale: The public zone is any network the administrator does not control, so the squadron's own web server is not placed there.

answers.text: Visitor network in the private zone; web server in the public zone.
answers.rationale: The private zone is where the Local Area Network (LAN) resides, which visitors typically do not need, and the public zone is a network the administrator does not control.

questions.stem: Two partner agencies must reach a shared reporting server over the Internet, and the general public must not. An airman proposes placing it in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) because it already admits Internet traffic. MSgt Rush must choose a security zone for the server. Which choice is best supported?

answers.text: Place it in the private zone, since it is shielded from other networks.
answers.rationale: The firewall in front of the private zone sends no traffic from any other network to it, so the partner agencies could not reach the server there.
Servers that the public must reach are placed in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), but the general public must not use this server.

answers.text: Place it in the public zone, since partners reach the Internet from there.
answers.rationale: The public zone is any network the administrator does not control, so a server meant for partners is not placed there.

answers.text: Place it in the extranet, since it holds servers for selected organizations.
answers.rationale: An extranet includes servers made accessible to selected organizations via the Internet, unlike servers that the public must reach, which belong in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

questions.stem: The squadron's wireless network is used by airmen who must reach the Internet and the extranet but not the private Local Area Network (LAN). An airman proposes placing the wireless network in the guest zone because it already limits what visitors reach. MSgt Rush must choose a zone for it. Which choice is best supported?

keywords.text: must reach the Internet and the extranet

answers.text: Place it in the guest zone, since it already limits what visitors reach.
answers.rationale: A guest zone has access to the public zone but none of the other security zones, so the airmen could not reach the extranet from it.

answers.text: Place it in the private zone, since the firewall there shields it from other networks.
answers.rationale: The private zone is where the Local Area Network (LAN) resides, which the airmen must not reach, so the wireless network would sit on it.

answers.text: Place it in a zone of its own, since the firewall decides which zones it reaches.
answers.rationale: A wireless network in a security zone of its own lets the firewall administrator control which zones its clients reach, whereas a guest zone has access to the public zone only.
Servers that the public must reach are placed in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ); it is not a security zone for a wireless network that needs the extranet.

questions.stem: Activity on a base server was first categorized as Investigating because its cause was unclear. Analysis now shows that malicious code on the server gave an attacker remote interactive control along with account credentials that can perform administrative functions. MSgt Rush proposes closing the case as Malicious Logic. Which category is best supported?

keywords.text: gave an attacker remote interactive control

answers.text: Malicious Logic, since the activity began when malicious code was installed on the server.
answers.rationale: How the activity began does not settle the category; malicious code that allowed remote interactive access is reported as an intrusion, not malicious logic.

answers.text: Root-Level Intrusion, since the code gave remote interactive control with administrative credentials.
answers.rationale: Malicious code that provides remote interactive control, with credentials that perform administrative functions, is reported as a root-level intrusion, not as malicious logic.

answers.text: Malicious Logic, since the code gave remote interactive control with administrative credentials.
answers.rationale: Malicious logic covers only code that gives no remote interactive control; code that allowed interactive access belongs in an intrusion category.

answers.text: Root-Level Intrusion, since the activity began when malicious code was installed on the server.
answers.rationale: Installing malicious code alone is malicious logic; the remote interactive control with administrative credentials is what puts this in the root-level category.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush is setting up incident handling for a newly formed unit that has no response arrangements yet. An airman proposes starting by writing the incident response plan, which will define each member's job role. Which first step is best supported?

keywords.text: starting by writing the incident response plan

answers.text: Write the incident response plan first, since the plan creates the team and names its members.
answers.rationale: The plan is developed once the team is in place; it does not create the team or name its members.

answers.text: Put the response team in place first, since the plan is developed after it to define roles.
answers.rationale: The first preparation step is having an incident response team in place; the plan is then developed to define each member's job role.

answers.text: Run a response exercise first, since exercise planning is the opening preparation step.
answers.rationale: Exercise planning is only one element of the plan, which does not yet exist for this unit, so practice cannot come first.

answers.text: Define the incident categories first, since the categories decide which members the team needs.
answers.rationale: Incident categories are an element of the plan, which is developed once the team is in place, so they cannot decide who joins it.

questions.stem: During a forensic review of an infected server, MSgt Rush must decide who answers a question about the regulations the organization must follow for computer forensics. The review may also need a contact at an outside agency that could be called upon in special circumstances. Which assignment is best supported?

keywords.text: who answers a question about the regulations

answers.text: The Technical Specialist answers the regulation question; the Team Leader builds the outside agency relationship.
answers.rationale: The Technical Specialist assesses the situation and the scale of the incident, so the regulation question does not belong to that role.

answers.text: The Legal Advisor answers the regulation question; the Team Leader builds the outside agency relationship.
answers.rationale: The Legal Advisor knows the laws and regulations for computer forensics, and the Team Leader builds relationships with outside resources that may be called upon.

answers.text: The Legal Advisor answers the regulation question; the Documentation Specialist builds the outside agency relationship.
answers.rationale: The Documentation Specialist logs each incident with its cause and solution; building relationships with outside resources is not that role's job.

answers.text: The Technical Specialist answers the regulation question; the Documentation Specialist builds the outside agency relationship.
answers.rationale: The Technical Specialist assesses the incident and the Documentation Specialist logs it, so neither answers the regulation question or builds outside relationships, which are other roles' duties.

questions.stem: An airman is the first person notified that systems on a base network are replicating a worm out to the Internet. The airman wonders whether to wait for a full assessment of the scale before acting. Which action is best supported?

answers.text: Wait for a full assessment of the scale, since the first responder just reports the incident to the team.
answers.rationale: A first responder takes charge of the incident rather than just reporting it, and the primary goal is to contain it.

answers.text: Activate the response team and contain the spread, since a first responder takes charge of the incident.
answers.rationale: The first responder takes charge, and the primary goal of activating the team and containing the incident can mean disconnecting from the Internet to stop a worm.

answers.text: Contain the spread but leave out the response team, since a first responder is not a member of it.
answers.rationale: The first responder is a member of the incident response team, so leaving the team out is not how the role works.

answers.text: Begin documenting the cause first, since the first responder's primary goal is logging the incident.
answers.rationale: Logging each incident is a separate documentation duty, not the first responder's primary goal of activating the team and containing the incident.

questions.stem: A case was opened as Investigating because its cause was unclear. Review now shows that an airman with an authorized account never applied required security patches, which exposed a server; no outsider gained access. MSgt Rush wants to close the case as Investigating. Which step is best supported?

answers.text: Close it as Investigating, since the cause is now known and nothing remains to review on the server.
answers.rationale: No event is closed out as Investigating; it is re-categorized before closure, even after the cause is known.

answers.text: Re-categorize it as User-Level Intrusion, since the airman's account reached the exposed server.
answers.rationale: User-level intrusion is unauthorized access, but the airman has an authorized account.

answers.text: Re-categorize it as Non-Compliance Activity, since an authorized user's inaction exposed the server.
answers.rationale: Failing to apply security patches is non-compliance activity by an authorized user, and no event is closed out as Investigating without being re-categorized.

answers.text: Re-categorize it as Explained Anomaly, since no outsider caused the exposure.
answers.rationale: An explained anomaly applies only when no other category fits, and a more specific category fits the missed patches here.

questions.stem: Logs show someone outside the network repeatedly trying valid username and password combinations against an airman's account. Normal defensive mechanisms blocked every attempt, and the attacker never gained access. MSgt Rush must record both the category and whether it is an event or an incident. Which entry is best supported?

keywords.text: repeatedly trying valid username and password combinations

answers.text: An event in the Reconnaissance category, since the attacker is probing for information about the account.
answers.rationale: Repeated attempts with valid or potentially valid credentials are not exploratory scanning, so this is not information gathering.

answers.text: An event in the Unsuccessful Activity Attempt category, since normal defenses defeated deliberate attempts.
answers.rationale: Deliberate attempts with valid or potentially valid credentials that normal defensive mechanisms defeat are an unsuccessful activity attempt, listed as an event.

answers.text: An incident in the Unsuccessful Activity Attempt category, since the attacker deliberately tried to gain access.
answers.rationale: The category is right, but an unsuccessful activity attempt is listed as an event, not an incident, because the attempts were defeated.

answers.text: An incident in the User-Level Intrusion category, since the attacker used credentials that belong to a user account.
answers.rationale: User-level intrusion requires unauthorized access, but the attacker never gained access.

questions.stem: A flood of requests has slowed a base web server to a crawl for hours, degrading its normal functionality. After review, MSgt Rush confirms that the slowdown actually jeopardizes the availability of the system. How should the activity be classified?

keywords.text: slowed a base web server to a crawl

answers.text: As an event in the Denial of Service category, since a flood of requests is merely an observable occurrence.
answers.rationale: The occurrence has been assessed as jeopardizing availability, so it is an incident, not merely an observable occurrence.

answers.text: As an incident in the Denial of Service category, since it degrades functionality and jeopardizes availability.
answers.rationale: Activity that degrades normal functionality is denial of service, and an assessed occurrence that jeopardizes availability is an incident.

answers.text: As an incident in the Reconnaissance category, since the review gathered information about the server and its users.
answers.rationale: Reconnaissance gathers information to formulate an attack; a flood that slows the server degrades its functionality instead.

answers.text: As an event in the Reconnaissance category, since the flood has not been assessed as harmful.
answers.rationale: The review confirmed the harm, so the activity is assessed, and a flood that degrades functionality is not reconnaissance.

questions.stem: Network technicians have just contained a threat on an affected server, and the local communications focal point wants to publish the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) for restoration immediately. MSgt Rush wants to confirm where this work belongs. Which statement is best supported?

keywords.text: just contained a threat on an affected server

answers.text: Containment completes Response and Recovery, so the restoration plan can go out now.
answers.rationale: Containment is a preliminary response action, not the completion of Response and Recovery, where the restoration plan is developed later.

answers.text: Containment is a preliminary response, so the restoration plan belongs to later Response and Recovery.
answers.rationale: Containment is a preliminary response action, and the local communications focal point develops the restoration plan in Response and Recovery, after more thorough analysis.

answers.text: The restoration plan is a postmortem product, so it waits for Post-Incident Analysis.
answers.rationale: The restoration plan is developed during Response and Recovery to guide system restoration, not by the postmortem that reviews the handling afterward.

answers.text: Containment and the restoration plan both belong to Preliminary Response Actions, so it can be published now.
answers.rationale: Preliminary response actions are immediate steps, with more steps after a thorough analysis, so the restoration plan is a later Response and Recovery product, not one of them.

questions.stem: An airman has gathered logs and personal accounts about an incident and wants to move straight to determining the operational impact. MSgt Rush notes that the reported details have not yet been checked against each other. Which next step is best supported?

keywords.text: reported details have not yet been checked against each other

answers.text: Coordinate with the owning support offices now, since coordination precedes the impact step in the process.
answers.rationale: Coordinate is the fourth step, taken after the operational impact is determined, not before.

answers.text: Determine reporting requirements now, since that step directly follows gathering information.
answers.rationale: Determining reporting requirements is the fifth and last step, and it does not follow gathering information.

answers.text: Validate the incident by corroborating the report, since validation precedes the impact step.
answers.rationale: Personnel continuously review, corroborate and update the reported incident in the second step, which comes before determining the operational impact.

answers.text: Gather the information again, since validation is the first of the five steps.
answers.rationale: Gathering information is the first step and has been done, so it is not the next step; validation is the second.

questions.stem: A cyber attack on a base server is still in progress. An airman suggests waiting for the postmortem to learn what happened and its root cause. MSgt Rush disagrees. Which approach is best supported?

answers.text: Wait for the postmortem, since that phase finds the root cause while an event continues.
answers.rationale: The postmortem reviews how the attack was handled after it ends, so it does not find the root cause while the event continues.

answers.text: Begin incident analysis now, since it finds the root cause while the event is in progress.
answers.rationale: Incident analysis finds out what happened, including the root cause, while the event is in progress, and post-incident analysis later reviews the handling.

answers.text: Wait for Response and Recovery, since that phase analyzes the event while it is in progress.
answers.rationale: Response and recovery restores systems and prevents recurrence; it does not perform the root cause analysis.

answers.text: Begin the postmortem now, since that phase runs while the event is still in progress.
answers.rationale: The postmortem is a review that happens after the handling is done, so starting it now would not reach the ongoing attack.

questions.stem: After an intrusion, MSgt Rush must produce two items: a detailed analysis of the affected systems, probable attackers and attack vectors used, and a report that focuses on a foreign group identified as a potential threat to Department of Defense (DoD) networks. Which pairing is best supported?

keywords.text: a report that focuses on a foreign group

answers.text: A Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) for the analysis; a postmortem for the foreign group.
answers.rationale: A Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) guides restoration and a postmortem reviews the handling afterward, so the first is not an analysis of the incident and the second is not a report on the foreign group.

answers.text: A Cyber Incident Report (CIR) for the analysis; a Network Intelligence Report (NIR) for the foreign group.
answers.rationale: The Cyber Incident Report (CIR) is the detailed analysis of affected systems, probable attackers and attack vectors, and the Network Intelligence Report (NIR) is the report that focuses on a foreign threat.

answers.text: A Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) for the analysis; a Network Intelligence Report (NIR) for the foreign group.
answers.rationale: A Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) lists restoration actions and responsible offices; it is not a detailed analysis of affected systems and attackers.

answers.text: A Cyber Incident Report (CIR) for the analysis; a postmortem for the foreign group.
answers.rationale: A postmortem captures lessons learned and missing policies afterward; it is not a report that focuses on a foreign threat.

questions.stem: During a sensitive operation, MSgt Rush learns that an adversary is still active on a network that the operation is watching to gain actionable intelligence. An airman, acting as first responder, wants to disconnect the affected systems immediately. Which response is best supported?

answers.text: Disconnect the systems immediately, since the first responder's goal of containment applies to this operation as well.
answers.rationale: Containment is the first responder's primary goal, but the operation's sensitivity can let adversary activity continue, so immediate disconnection is not required.

answers.text: Power off the network switch to stop the adversary activity, since a first responder stops the spread of adversary activity.
answers.rationale: Powering off a switch is the example for a worm replicating out to the Internet; a sensitive operation may instead let the adversary activity continue.

answers.text: Let the adversary activity continue, since a sensitive operation can deviate from typical handling to gain intelligence.
answers.rationale: A sensitive operation may deviate from typical cyber incident handling, and adversary activity may be allowed to continue to gain actionable intelligence.

answers.text: Categorize the activity as Explained Anomaly, since the operation expects the adversary to be there.
answers.rationale: An explained anomaly is non-malicious activity, and an active adversary is not, so the category does not fit.

questions.stem: Several airmen disagree about when to report a suspicious pop-up and about who should be told first. MSgt Rush wants the written incident response plan to settle both questions. Which addition is best supported?

keywords.text: when to report a suspicious pop-up

answers.text: Add incident categories, since they tell users when and how to report an incident to the response team.
answers.rationale: Incident categories define the different types of security incidents; they do not say when users report or who receives the report.

answers.text: Add exercise planning, since practice sessions settle when users report and to whom.
answers.rationale: Exercise planning arranges practice of the response; it does not identify when users report or who the first responder is.

answers.text: Add reporting requirements and escalation, since they name when users report and the first responder.
answers.rationale: The plan identifies when and how users report potential security incidents and who the first responder is to escalate the incident to.

answers.text: Add roles and responsibilities, since they name the first responder that users report to.
answers.rationale: Roles and responsibilities define each member's job role before, during and after an incident; they do not say when and how users report.

questions.stem: A compromise destroyed mission-critical data. MSgt Rush must prepare an impact assessment and also determine the system's Mission Assurance Category level. Two contacts are available: the HQ USAF Damage Assessment Management Office (AF-DAMO) and the system's owning support offices. Which pairing is best supported?

answers.text: The owning support offices for the impact assessment; the damage assessment office for the level.
answers.rationale: These assignments are reversed: help with the impact assessment comes from the damage assessment office, not the owning support offices, which set the level.

answers.text: The damage assessment office for both the impact assessment and the level.
answers.rationale: The level is determined by coordinating with the owning support offices, not with the damage assessment office.

answers.text: The damage assessment office for the impact assessment; the owning support offices for the level.
answers.rationale: Personnel coordinate with the damage assessment office for help preparing an impact assessment, and with the owning support offices to determine the level.

answers.text: The owning support offices for both the impact assessment and the level.
answers.rationale: Help preparing an impact assessment comes from the damage assessment office, not from the owning support offices.

questions.stem: A sensor alert on a workstation was categorized as Investigating. Review finds that a failing disk caused the alert and that nothing else fits. MSgt Rush must file the case. Which filing is best supported?

keywords.text: a failing disk caused the alert

answers.text: Non-Compliance Activity, noting the reason, since a failing disk exposes the workstation to increased risk.
answers.rationale: Non-compliance activity comes from the action or inaction of authorized users, and a failing disk is neither.

answers.text: Explained Anomaly, with no reason added, since a failing disk is a system malfunction.
answers.rationale: Events in this category are reported with the reason specified, so filing one without a reason skips that requirement.

answers.text: Reconnaissance, noting the reason, since the alert showed information being gathered about the workstation.
answers.rationale: Reconnaissance gathers information to formulate an attack; a failing disk is not information gathering.

answers.text: Explained Anomaly, noting the reason it fits no other category, since a failing disk is a system malfunction.
answers.rationale: A system malfunction found non-malicious that fits no other category is an explained anomaly, and its report specifies why it cannot be otherwise categorized.

questions.stem: A new authentication server has room for only two drives. MSgt Rush wants its data to survive the failure of either drive, while an airman proposes striping to boost performance. Which technique best fits the server?

keywords.text: survive the failure of either drive

answers.text: Striping, since dividing the data between both drives boosts performance.
answers.rationale: Striping has no redundancy, so if either drive fails, all the data is permanently lost.

answers.text: Mirroring, since each of the two drives holds an exact duplicate of the data.
answers.rationale: Mirroring reflects all data on one drive onto the other, needs only two drives and suits data that must be retained, such as on authentication servers.

answers.text: Parity, since a parity bit lets the server rebuild the data from a failed drive.
answers.rationale: Parity can rebuild one failed drive, but it needs at least three disks, and this server holds two.

answers.text: Double parity, since it lets the server rebuild the data after two drives fail.
answers.rationale: Double parity needs at least four disks, more than the two this server can hold.

questions.stem: A server holds so much data that a full backup would fill the whole overnight window, so full backups run only on weekends. An airman wants the shortest weekday backup each night and treats restore effort as secondary. MSgt Rush suggests differential backups because a restore needs few backup sets. Which weekday approach best meets the airman's goal?

answers.text: Incremental backups, since each one copies only the data changed since the previous backup.
answers.rationale: Incremental backups back up all data that has changed since the previous backup, so less data is backed up each time and they are relatively fast.

answers.text: Differential backups, since a restore needs only the most recent full backup and the most recent differential.
answers.rationale: Differential backups are faster to restore, but they take longer to perform because more data is backed up every time.

answers.text: Incremental backups, since a restore needs only the full backup and the newest incremental backup.
answers.rationale: Incremental backups do take more time to restore, because the full backup must be restored first followed by every incremental backup in the order they were made.

answers.text: Differential backups, since each one clears the archive bit and stays small.
answers.rationale: Differential backups do not clear the archive bit, and they take longer each time because more data is backed up.

questions.stem: A unit builds two storage servers. One holds an email archive on three drives. The other runs application servers with a fast database on four drives. MSgt Rush wants Level 1+0 on both servers for simplicity, and an airman proposes Level 5 on both. Which assignment best fits?

answers.text: Level 1+0 for both servers, since it combines striping and mirroring and suits both uses.
answers.rationale: Level 1+0 requires a minimum of four disks, and the email archive has only three drives.

answers.text: Level 5 for both servers, since parity rebuilds a failed drive and the archive needs just three disks.
answers.rationale: Level 5 is commonly used for email archives, but Level 1+0 is the level commonly used for application servers and fast databases.

answers.text: Level 5 for the email archive and Level 1+0 for the application server, since each level fits its use and its disk count.
answers.rationale: Level 5 requires a minimum of three disks and is commonly used for email archives, and Level 1+0 requires four and suits application servers and fast databases.

answers.text: Level 1+0 for the email archive and Level 5 for the application server, since mirroring protects archives.
answers.rationale: Level 1+0 requires four disks, which the three-drive archive lacks, and it is the level commonly used for application servers and fast databases.

questions.stem: An airman must reformat the hard drive of a Department of Defense (DoD) laptop and load new software. The laptop holds important mission files. MSgt Rush suggests copying the files to a detachable drive kept offline. The airman suggests reformatting now and dealing with the files afterward. What is the best course?

answers.text: Copy the files to a detachable drive kept offline before reformatting, since offline storage is the usual advice for personal backups.
Back up the files to cloud storage and shared network drives before reformatting, since removable storage is typically not permitted.
answers.rationale: Customers should back up data before major changes like reformatting, and because removable storage is typically not permitted on Department of Defense (DoD) computers, the backup goes to cloud storage and shared network drives.

answers.text: Reformat the drive now and back up the files afterward, since the new software will protect the existing mission files.
answers.rationale: Backups come before major changes such as reformatting a hard drive, because data that is lost with no backup cannot be recovered.

answers.text: Skip the backup altogether, since programs can be reloaded after the reformat and the files will come back with them.
answers.rationale: Programs seldom change and can be reloaded, but data changes constantly and cannot be recovered if it is lost with no backup.

questions.stem: A server was baselined when it was built. After a patch, a new measurement shows two known weaknesses fixed and none added. MSgt Rush says nothing got worse, so there is no deviation to record. An airman wants to keep measuring against the original baseline. What is the best assessment?

answers.text: Record no deviation and keep the original baseline, since just the changes that raise risk count as deviations.
answers.rationale: A baseline deviation is a change from the original baseline value, and the change can be positive, like lowering risk, or negative, like increasing risk.

answers.text: Record a positive deviation and evaluate it for remediation as new risk, since a deviation from the baseline needs that evaluation.
answers.rationale: Only a change that increases risk needs evaluating for possible remediation, and this patch lowered risk.

answers.text: Stop baselining the server, since the patch already measured its state of security readiness.
answers.rationale: Baselining is the measuring of a system's current state of security readiness, and after changes the baseline is measured again to look for deviations.

answers.text: Record a positive deviation and update the baseline, since a deviation can lower risk and updates require a current baseline.
answers.rationale: A baseline deviation is a change from the original baseline value that can lower risk, and the baseline configuration requires updating to keep it current as updates are applied.

questions.stem: A differential backup of a file server finished Tuesday night. An airman expects Wednesday night's differential to hold just the files changed since Tuesday, because Tuesday's backup reset the archive bit. MSgt Rush disagrees. What does Wednesday night's differential back up?

answers.text: Everything changed since the last full backup, since a differential does not clear the archive bit.
answers.rationale: Differential backups copy everything changed since the most recent full backup and do not clear the archive bit, so Tuesday's changed files are still marked as not backed up.

answers.text: Just the files changed since Tuesday night, since a differential clears the archive bit as each file is copied.
answers.rationale: Clearing the archive bit is what full and incremental backups do; differential backups do NOT clear it.

answers.text: The whole server contents, since a differential repeats a full backup each night.
answers.rationale: A full backup copies all files and folders, while a differential copies only what changed since the most recent full backup.

answers.text: Nothing, since files already backed up have an archive bit of zero and are skipped.
answers.rationale: A zero archive bit means a file has been backed up, but a differential leaves the bit set, so the changed files are copied again.

questions.stem: A squadron has gathered and recorded its inventories, forms, policies, equipment lists and contact details for IT disaster recovery planning. MSgt Rush wants to test the plan now. An airman wants to prioritize the processes again. What should the squadron do next?

answers.text: Test the plan now, since the collected data is enough to show how effective the plan will be in a real disaster and what changes it needs.
answers.rationale: Testing the plan is the sixth and last step, so it comes after the plan has been created.

answers.text: Create the plan in a standard format, since data collection is complete and testing needs an existing plan to test.
answers.rationale: Creating the plan is the fifth step, after data collection, and uses a standard format that details procedures and includes essential information.

answers.text: Prioritize the processes again, since process categories get set after the data has been collected.
answers.rationale: Prioritizing processes and operations is the third step and comes before data collection, which is the fourth step.

answers.text: Assemble the team again, since the data was gathered without core members from the departments.
answers.rationale: Assembling the team is the first step, which comes before data collection rather than after it.

questions.stem: A unit adds new records to a critical database every hour. MSgt Rush must set how often to back up and what type of backup to run. An airman must choose between electronic vaulting and mirrored disks as the method. Which pairing of deciding factors is correct?

answers.text: Base frequency and type on media size, cost and speed, and the method on how critical the data is.
answers.rationale: Media size, cost and speed decide what to store backed-up data on, not how often to back up or which type to run.

answers.text: Base frequency, type and method on the availability and integrity requirements of the systems.
answers.rationale: Frequency, type and method are not all decided by the same factors; this pairing gives one pair of factors to all three decisions.

answers.text: Base frequency and type on availability and integrity, and the method on data criticality and the rate of new records.
answers.rationale: This reverses the pairing: the factors named for frequency and type belong to the method, and the method factors belong to frequency and type.

answers.text: Base frequency and type on data criticality and update rate, and the method on availability and integrity.
answers.rationale: Policies set the frequency and type of backup by data criticality and how often new information is introduced, while the method is based on system and data availability and integrity requirements.

questions.stem: An airman wants every user on the unit network to be able to adjust the firewall settings so people can fix their own connection problems, and sees no need for a firewall on a personal home network because the unit already has one. MSgt Rush sets the policy. Which policy is best?

answers.text: Keep the settings with network administrators and add a home firewall, since users should not tamper with settings and home networks need one.
answers.rationale: Firewalls are typically managed by network administrators, users should not tamper with firewall settings, and it is recommended that users implement a firewall on their personal home networks.

answers.text: Give users access to the firewall settings and skip the home firewall, since the unit firewall already protects the airman's connection.
answers.rationale: Users should not be given access to firewall settings, and a firewall is recommended on personal home networks.

answers.text: Give users access to the firewall settings but require a home firewall, since users know their own connections best.
answers.rationale: Users should not be given access to firewall settings or be able to tamper with them, even though a home firewall is recommended.

answers.text: Keep the settings with network administrators but skip the home firewall, since personal networks are outside the unit's concern.
answers.rationale: Keeping settings with administrators is right, but it is recommended that users implement a firewall on their personal home networks.

questions.stem: An airman keeps canceling the security scans that slow a laptop and puts off the restart that the antivirus software requests after new virus definitions arrive. MSgt Rush must correct the habit. Which correction is best?

answers.text: Let the scans finish but skip the restarts, since administrators scan the whole network from a central point anyway.
answers.rationale: Administrators scan from a central point regularly, but users must still install updates and restart their machines when prompted.

answers.text: Let the scans finish and install updates when administrators patch the laptop remotely, since they handle patching centrally.
answers.rationale: Administrators can remotely patch devices as necessary, but users should still allow automatic updates and restart their machine when prompted.

answers.text: Let the scans finish and install updates when prompted, since users should not interfere and should keep definitions current.
answers.rationale: Users should allow scans to happen and not interfere with them, and should allow automatic updates and restart their machine when prompted.

answers.text: Let the updates install but cancel the scans, since a restart already applies the new virus definitions.
answers.rationale: Antivirus software should regularly perform security scans, and users should allow them to happen rather than cancel them.

questions.stem: A server's data is critical, and the unit wants it rebuilt after any two of its four drives crash. MSgt Rush proposes striping for speed. An airman proposes a single parity bit. Which technique best meets the requirement?

keywords.text: any two of its four drives

answers.text: Striping, since dividing the data between the four drives boosts performance on a busy server.
answers.rationale: Striping has no redundancy, so one failed drive loses all of the data.

answers.text: Double parity, since two redundant disks allow a rebuild after two drives crash and four disks meet its minimum.
answers.rationale: Double parity gives two redundant disks, so the parity and remaining data can rebuild the lost data if two drives crash, and it requires a minimum of four disks.

answers.text: Parity, since a single parity bit lets the remaining data rebuild the lost data when a drive crashes.
answers.rationale: A single parity bit gives one redundant disk, so only one failed drive can be rebuilt.

answers.text: Striped mirrors, since combining striping with mirroring across the four disks adds redundancy against a second drive crash.
answers.rationale: Combining striping and mirroring needs four disks, but it is not described as rebuilding data after two drives crash.

questions.stem: An airman sets up password-management software and uses a dictionary word with a few letters swapped for numbers as the master password, the same one used on the unit email service, so it is easy to remember. MSgt Rush reviews the choice. What is the best correction?

answers.text: Keep it, since the software encrypts the wallet whatever master password is chosen.
answers.rationale: The wallet is protected by a single master password, which should be long and strong, so a weak one defeats the protection.

answers.text: Keep the word but make it longer and keep the email match, since longer is better and the swapped letters then stop mattering.
answers.rationale: Replacing a single letter in a dictionary word with a number is an obvious substitution, and the master password should not be duplicated elsewhere.

answers.text: Reuse the email password but add symbols, since a mix of characters makes the password stronger.
Pick a master password that is long and strong and not reused, since obvious substitutions are easy to crack.
answers.rationale: Obvious substitutions in dictionary words are easy to crack, and the master password should be long and strong and not duplicated elsewhere.

questions.stem: A unit must stand up many new servers that all match the approved system settings. An airman proposes configuring each one by hand. MSgt Rush proposes copying the first server and adjusting each copy as needed. Which approach best uses configuration management?

keywords.text: all match the approved system settings

answers.text: Define settings once from the baseline and deploy with tools, since tools make deployments repeatable and scalable.
answers.rationale: Configuration management lets you define system settings and build systems in line with your baseline, and its tools make deployments repeatable and scalable.

answers.text: Configure each server by hand from a checklist, since careful manual work on each server keeps the servers matching the approved baseline.
answers.rationale: Hand configuration is not what configuration management tools provide, and undocumented differences across many systems result in instability and downtime.

answers.text: Copy the first server to the others and adjust each copy, since the first server already matches the approved settings.
answers.rationale: Adjusting each copy creates undocumented changes, and when undocumented changes occur across many systems and applications, instability and downtime are the result.

answers.text: Build each server from its defaults and roll back the ones that fail, since a rollback restores a configuration that worked.
answers.rationale: A rollback returns a system to the previous configuration that worked; it is a recovery benefit and not a way to build servers to the baseline.

questions.stem: An airman downloads a patch from a vendor site that lists the file's hash value. The airman runs the file through the same hashing algorithm and gets a different value. MSgt Rush suggests installing the patch anyway, since the download finished without errors. Which action is best supported?

answers.text: Install the patch despite the different hash value, since a download that ends without errors arrives unaltered.
answers.rationale: Finishing without errors says nothing about integrity; the integrity check compares the vendor's hash value with the one calculated after downloading.

answers.text: Do not install the patch, since the differing hash values show the file changed in transit.
answers.rationale: Matching hash values mean the data has not been altered, so a value that differs from the vendor's listed hash shows the downloaded file changed.

answers.text: Install the patch after encrypting it, since encryption keeps its contents from changing.
answers.rationale: Encryption keeps information unreadable to unauthorized people; it does not undo or detect a change already made to the file.

answers.text: Do not install the patch until it is encrypted, since encryption proves the file is unaltered.
answers.rationale: Encryption protects confidentiality, not integrity; it proves nothing about whether the downloaded file was altered.

questions.stem: An order that changed a duty roster was sent from an airman's account. The airman denies sending it. The logs show that the message was signed with the airman's private key, which only the airman can use. MSgt Rush must decide what the logs establish. Which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: The airman can dispute sending it, since a digital signature shows just that the message was not altered.
answers.rationale: A digital signature is created with the sender's private key to prove who sent the message, not only to show that it is unaltered.

answers.text: The airman cannot dispute sending it, since a digital signature made with the airman's private key proves the sender.
answers.rationale: Only the airman has the private key, so the signature proves the sender is who they say they are, and signatures implement nonrepudiation.

answers.text: The airman cannot dispute sending it, since encrypting the message keeps it unreadable to everyone else.
answers.rationale: Encryption puts information in an unreadable format until an authorized person decrypts it; it does not tie the message to a particular sender.

answers.text: The airman can dispute sending it, since a digital certificate merely transports keys and names no sender of any message.
answers.rationale: A digital certificate transports keys, but the signature made with the private key is what proves the sender, so the dispute fails.

questions.stem: A file server stores data on several drives that work together, and a mail service runs on two servers that act as one unit. One storage drive and one mail server fail at the same time, yet users keep reaching both services. MSgt Rush must report which availability solution covered each failure. Which report is best supported?

keywords.text: One storage drive and one mail server fail

answers.text: Clustering covered the failed drive and fault tolerance covered the failed mail server, because each kept its service running for the users.
answers.rationale: The solutions are reversed: other drives supplying missing data is fault tolerance, and another server taking over the workload is clustering.

answers.text: Backups covered both failures, because regular copies were restored the moment each component failed.
answers.rationale: Backups are restored after data becomes corrupt or unavailable; they do not keep a service reachable at the moment of failure.

answers.text: Fault tolerance covered both failures, because other drives supplied the missing data for each.
answers.rationale: Other drives supplying the missing data is fault tolerance; the failed mail server needed another server to take over the workload, which is clustering.

answers.text: Fault tolerance covered the failed drive and clustering covered the failed mail server, because each had a redundant counterpart.
answers.rationale: The other drives supplied the failed drive's data, which is fault tolerance, and the second server took over the workload, which is clustering.

questions.stem: An unauthorized person logged on to a unit workstation from a remote location by guessing a weak password. MSgt Rush must record the incident under the three vulnerability categories of the Air Force Computer Security (COMPUSEC) program and name the primary preventive measure. Which entry is best supported?

keywords.text: logged on to a unit workstation from a remote location

answers.text: Malicious logic, prevented primarily by password or Personal Identification Number (PIN) protection.
answers.rationale: Malicious logic is computer code written to cause problems, but the stem describes a person gaining access, which is unauthorized access.

answers.text: Unauthorized access, prevented primarily by locking switches and routers in a communications closet.
answers.rationale: Locking network links in closets is a secure area access control, which is described as another way, not the primary means.

answers.text: Unauthorized access, prevented primarily by password or Personal Identification Number (PIN) protection.
answers.rationale: A person gaining access to a system is unauthorized access, most often by remote hacking, and password or Personal Identification Number (PIN) protection is the primary means of preventing it.

answers.text: Malicious logic, prevented primarily by locking switches and routers in a communications closet.
answers.rationale: Malicious logic is computer code written to cause problems, but the stem describes a person gaining access, and locking network links in closets is described as another way, not the primary means.

questions.stem: An airman argues that a standalone workstation that processes national security information, never connected to any network, needs no emanation review because nothing can reach it. MSgt Rush must decide whether the airman is correct. Which assessment is best supported?

answers.text: The airman is right, since without a network connection the workstation gives off no signals that could be intercepted by anyone outside the room.
answers.rationale: Even computers not connected to network media can be eavesdropped upon by monitoring the electrical signals they emit.

answers.text: The airman is right, since proper design eliminates the unintentional signals of an unconnected computer.
answers.rationale: Proper design minimizes the unintentional signals, but some unintentional signals will always be present.

answers.text: The airman is wrong, since the workstation gives off electromagnetic signals that can be intercepted even without a network connection.
